$$

$$

Let $F(x)=5{x}^{2}+1$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=5{x}^{2}+1$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(5{x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{[\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3}+x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{5{\pi }^{3}}{3}+\pi )-0 \\  & =2(\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{3}+1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fdceacd7-e832-59cd-b2a8-3585e4638dba"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fdceacd7-e832-59cd-b2a8-3585e4638dba" :answer-field/id #uuid "fdceacd7-e832-59cd-b2a8-3585e4638dba" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-72a81ffa-dc5e-51a3-a7da-856e67b88f39" :answer-field/choices ["answer-72a81ffa-dc5e-51a3-a7da-856e67b88f39"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-72a81ffa-dc5e-51a3-a7da-856e67b88f39" :answer/id #uuid "72a81ffa-dc5e-51a3-a7da-856e67b88f39" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2(\frac{5\pi^{2}}{3}+1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-6da2a50a-0f62-59bb-a9db-a784f084c0f1" :question/id #uuid "6da2a50a-0f62-59bb-a9db-a784f084c0f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-341277" :question/problem "$$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by

In our case, $f(x)=6{x}^{2}+1$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-989a790f-36d6-537f-bac0-75e070b26f48"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-989a790f-36d6-537f-bac0-75e070b26f48" :answer-field/id #uuid "989a790f-36d6-537f-bac0-75e070b26f48" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-50462a04-0887-512d-8b96-cd650e92389f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-50462a04-0887-512d-8b96-cd650e92389f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-50462a04-0887-512d-8b96-cd650e92389f" :answer/id #uuid "50462a04-0887-512d-8b96-cd650e92389f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\pi^{2}+2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186314316 :answer-field/correct "answer-07aa64d0-a645-5949-a1b8-1717374a9409" :answer-field/choices ["answer-07aa64d0-a645-5949-a1b8-1717374a9409"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-07aa64d0-a645-5949-a1b8-1717374a9409" :answer/id #uuid "07aa64d0-a645-5949-a1b8-1717374a9409" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2(\frac{5\pi^{2}}{3}+2)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186372764 :question/problem "$$

$$
f(x)∼(-4+\frac{7\pi }{2})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=7x-4$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(7x-4)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=7x-4\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=7 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(7x-4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{7}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((7\pi -4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{7}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{7}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{14(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{14((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(-4+\frac{7\pi }{2})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{14((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d8649ec8-1d2d-592d-8063-88c05a6c45a3" "answer-field-e947fd84-1d63-5d10-af30-150e8c1aaa94"] :db/ensure \begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(4x-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{4}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((4\pi -1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{4}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{4}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{8((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(-1+2\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{8((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-98620a41-f0fa-569b-a3ec-5642c8206fa4" "answer-field-901c601c-f36e-56ff-8079-21f7d8654a35"] :db/ensure Let $F(x)=-8x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{n}.$

for $n\ge 1$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168044 :tutorial/content "In the earlier topics, we saw that *symmetry* can force many Fourier coefficients to be zero automatically.
In particular, if a $2\pi$-periodic function is *even*, then its Fourier series has *cosine terms only*.

A **Fourier cosine series** uses this idea when a function is initially given only on the half-interval $[0,\pi),$ but we want a full Fourier series on $[-\pi,\pi)$ (and then a $2\pi$-periodic extension to all real $x$).

To do this, we start with a function $F(x)$ on $[0,\pi)$ and define its **even extension** $f(x)$ to $(-\pi,\pi)$ by
![](images/e2/e2e07048ac4750968947e45443f59096f395b159d4f7a846410a711194b11a14.svg)

For example, a function $F(x),$ defined on $x \in [0,1),$ and its even extension $f(x)$ to $x \in (-1,1)$ are shown below.

![](images/33/33d92f280a5672c8d9d94553ccc1ada2a9c5ea1ff12344ca8c9aeca9f44c40c6.png)

By construction, $f$ is an *even* function, meaning $f(-x)=f(x)$. Because $f$ is even, its Fourier series on $[-\pi,\pi)$ has *cosine terms only*:

$$
f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\cos(nx)
$$

Since $f(x)$ is even and $\cos(nx)$ is even for any $n\ge 1,$ the product $f(x)\cos(nx)$ is even too. Therefore, the cosine coefficients can be computed using the *half-range formulas*:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and for $n\ge 1,$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

So in practice, the workflow is the following:

1\. Start with $F$ on $[0,\pi)$ and form the even extension $f$ on $(-\pi,\pi).$

2\. Compute $a_0$ and $a_n$ from the half-range integrals on $[0,\pi).$

3\. Write the Fourier cosine series of $f.$

Let's see some concrete examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186271768 :answer-field/choices 17592186269568] [:db/retract 17592186271768 :answer-field/choices 17592186270849] [:db/retract 17592186271768 :answer-field/choices 17592186270659] [:db/retract 17592186271768 :answer-field/choices 17592186270793] [:db/retract 17592186271768 :answer-field/choices 17592186269356] [:db/retract 17592186271540 :answer-field/choices 17592186270456] [:db/retract 17592186271540 :answer-field/choices 17592186269522] [:db/retract 17592186271540 :answer-field/choices 17592186269432] [:db/retract 17592186271540 :answer-field/choices 17592186271177] [:db/retract 17592186271540 :answer-field/choices 17592186269789] {:db/id 17592186068874 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3846b0e4-266a-5fcc-97c9-5ac90ce8b7bf"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186272045 :question/worked-solution "First, we recall the following formula:

what is the value of $a+b?$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 2v & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & v \\ 2v & u\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & v \\ 0 & u\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x,\,y,\,xz⟩{|}_{x=u\,y={v}^{2}\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}v⟩\cdot ⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩ \\  & =u\cdot (-2{v}^{2})+{v}^{2}\cdot (-u)+{u}^{2}v\cdot 2v \\  & =-2u{v}^{2}-u{v}^{2}+2{u}^{2}{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}{v}^{2}-3u{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\cdot {u}^{2}{v}^{2}+(-3)\cdot u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=2-3=-1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-63772144-9630-582a-8d79-f08320bc64ad"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

The scatter plot above gives the correspondence between the variables $x$ and $y$ for some data points. Estimate the value of $y$ when $x=20.$ 

*Hint: Assume the trend is linear, and that the trend line passes through the points $(1,23)$ and $(9,27).$*" :question/worked-solution "First, using the hint, let's draw an approximate trend line for our scatter plot.

![](images/a0/a00942c18663c8e9ea2dd2c5354bbe177f7f8b35a4568c5234b9c92b844f196a.png)

Our trend line passes through $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(1,23)$ and $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(9,27).$

We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form 

$$
y=mx+b.
$$

First, we calculate the slope $m$ of the line as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{27-23}{9-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{8} \\  & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $m=0.5$ into the slope-intercept form above, we get

$$
y=0.5x+b.
$$

We now need to calculate the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can do this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(1,23):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =0.5x+b \\ 23 & =0.5(1)+b \\ 23 & =0.5+b \\ b & =22.5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=0.5x+22.5.
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=20$ into the equation above, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =0.5x+22.5 \\  & =0.5(20)+22.5 \\  & =10+22.5 \\  & =32.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, according to this model, when $x=20$ we have $y≈32.5.$

Note: The point where $x=20$ is not shown on our trend line. Therefore, our result *may* be unreliable." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1a665d06-44a7-566e-9ba1-44800e618b3b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1a665d06-44a7-566e-9ba1-44800e618b3b" :answer-field/id #uuid "1a665d06-44a7-566e-9ba1-44800e618b3b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5f18bd76-f921-5ef0-ab74-e55531698dd4" :answer-field/choices ["answer-528ae067-ae5a-58ad-a807-4a32664e9dd8" "answer-5a121c0e-eee5-5094-93d2-ed8591f7049e" "answer-5f18bd76-f921-5ef0-ab74-e55531698dd4" "answer-f96d4a56-8233-583c-bdd1-d33a53b4fcd4" "answer-3177c2c7-aa42-566a-8362-fecceb1e8163"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-528ae067-ae5a-58ad-a807-4a32664e9dd8" :answer/id #uuid "528ae067-ae5a-58ad-a807-4a32664e9dd8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "30.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5a121c0e-eee5-5094-93d2-ed8591f7049e" :answer/id #uuid "5a121c0e-eee5-5094-93d2-ed8591f7049e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "31" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5f18bd76-f921-5ef0-ab74-e55531698dd4" :answer/id #uuid "5f18bd76-f921-5ef0-ab74-e55531698dd4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f96d4a56-8233-583c-bdd1-d33a53b4fcd4" :answer/id #uuid "f96d4a56-8233-583c-bdd1-d33a53b4fcd4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "33" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3177c2c7-aa42-566a-8362-fecceb1e8163" :answer/id #uuid "3177c2c7-aa42-566a-8362-fecceb1e8163" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "34.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-73f7b139-c8da-5c53-9a35-10e77ca9a819" :question/id #uuid "73f7b139-c8da-5c53-9a35-10e77ca9a819" :question/math-academy-id "q-133962" :question/problem "![](images/6f/6f38e64442bb383f218dede5a88740653f958864d3284ce09c3e1bb99ed7e421.png)

The scatter plot above shows the relationship between the time (in hours) some college students spend studying the night before an exam and the time they spend sleeping that night. Assuming this trend continues, estimate the time a student spends studying if that student gets only $3.75$ hours of sleep.

*Hint: Assume the trend is linear and that the trend line passes through the points $(2,7.5)$ and $(4,5).$*" :question/worked-solution "First, using the hint, let's draw an approximate trend line for our scatter plot.

![](images/9e/9e1653b2acbe5c5924e2d562308b2640c64f317ed7500fba4e149c926c9205ab.png)

The trend line passes through $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,7.5)$ and $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(4,5).$

We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form 

$$
y=mx+b.
$$

First, we find the slope $m$ of the line as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{5-7.5}{4-2} \\  & =\frac{(-2.5)}{2} \\  & =-1.25\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $m=-1.25$ into the slope-intercept form above, we get

$$
y=-1.25x+b.
$$

We now need to calculate the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can do this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(4,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-1.25x+b \\ 5 & =-1.25(4)+b \\ 5 & =-5+b \\ b & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=-1.25x+10.
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=3.75$ into the equation above and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-1.25x+10 \\ 3.75 & =-1.25x+10 \\ 1.25x & =6.25 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, according to this model, the student spends approximately $5$ hours studying.

Note: The point where $y=3.75$ is not shown on our trend line. To do this, we subtract $4$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2mn+m+4 & =7 \\ 2mn+m+4-4 & =7-4 \\ 2mn+m & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor out $m$ in the expression on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2mn+m & =3 \\ m(2n+1) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $(2n+1)$ to isolate $m:$

$$

{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we isolate the absolute value on the left side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|1-2x|-2 & =7 \\ |1-2x| & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following two cases:

- If $|1-2x|=1-2x,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|1-2x| & =9 \\ 1-2x & =9 \\ -2x & =8 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|1-2x|=-(1-2x),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|1-2x| & =9 \\ -(1-2x) & =9 \\ -1+2x & =9 \\ 2x & =10 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the solutions are $x=-4$ and $x=5.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4805b999-73a4-56f9-85d1-fd39b746b678" "answer-field-551c716c-7245-54c5-b067-9d77aa114b1a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4805b999-73a4-56f9-85d1-fd39b746b678" :answer-field/id #uuid "4805b999-73a4-56f9-85d1-fd39b746b678" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-dad0e77a-e20e-537d-a75c-ebf6a272d4ad" :answer-field/choices ["answer-dad0e77a-e20e-537d-a75c-ebf6a272d4ad"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dad0e77a-e20e-537d-a75c-ebf6a272d4ad" :answer/id #uuid "dad0e77a-e20e-537d-a75c-ebf6a272d4ad" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-551c716c-7245-54c5-b067-9d77aa114b1a" :answer-field/id #uuid "551c716c-7245-54c5-b067-9d77aa114b1a" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-92345246-b68e-50d2-85cc-0c9a1ffea68e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-92345246-b68e-50d2-85cc-0c9a1ffea68e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-92345246-b68e-50d2-85cc-0c9a1ffea68e" :answer/id #uuid "92345246-b68e-50d2-85cc-0c9a1ffea68e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069424 :question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt[3]{-\frac{64}{{b}^{3}}}.$" :question/worked-solution "To simplify the expression, we write the term under the radical as a perfect cube, and simplify:

10$ is $a${{field-1}}{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "The variable $a$ is being *multiplied* by $-2.$ To isolate $a,$ we perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $-2.$ Remember Also, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2a\,\, & \ge \,\,10 \\ \frac{-2a}{-2}\,\, & \le \,\,\frac{10}{-2} \\ \frac{-2a}{-2}\,\, & \le \,\,-5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-2$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-2a}{-2} & \le -5 \\ \frac{\cancel{-2}a}{\cancel{-2}} & \le -5 \\ a & \le -5\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{12} & =\sqrt{4\cdot 3}=\sqrt{4}\cdot \sqrt{3}=2\sqrt{3} & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}4\sqrt{3}-5\sqrt{12} & = \\ 4\sqrt{3}-5(2\sqrt{3}) & = \\ 4\sqrt{3}-10\sqrt{3}. & \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can combine the two $\sqrt{3}$ terms together:

"If $v=2τdh,$ then $τ=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate $τ,$ so we will treat the other variables $v,d,$ and $h$ as constants. We can use the multiplication principle to solve for $τ.$

First, we rearrange and then divide both sides by $2dh:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =2τdh \\ v & =(2dh)τ \\ \frac{v}{2dh} & =\frac{(2dh)τ}{2dh} \\ \frac{v}{2dh} & =τ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $τ=\frac{v}{2dh}.$

**Note:** This result assumes that $d\ne 0$ and $h\ne 0.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-066b2166-822f-5d65-8ee3-2f1f64ae2d7d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-066b2166-822f-5d65-8ee3-2f1f64ae2d7d" :answer-field/id #uuid "066b2166-822f-5d65-8ee3-2f1f64ae2d7d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-71a54dfc-a7bc-50b1-888f-91e3d09fe8d3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-71a54dfc-a7bc-50b1-888f-91e3d09fe8d3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-71a54dfc-a7bc-50b1-888f-91e3d09fe8d3" :answer/id #uuid "71a54dfc-a7bc-50b1-888f-91e3d09fe8d3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{v}{2dh}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133921 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d9b9c93d-9a95-57ab-bfc8-b62b1c153ff8"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d9b9c93d-9a95-57ab-bfc8-b62b1c153ff8" :question/id #uuid "d9b9c93d-9a95-57ab-bfc8-b62b1c153ff8" :question/math-academy-id "q-63877" :question/problem "Evaluate $\sqrt[3]{5y+1}$ at $y=3.$" :question/worked-solution "We replace $y$ with $3$ in the given expression, and simplify as much as possible:

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

To plot $y=f(3(x+2)),$ we apply the following steps:

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{(3)}=\frac{1}{3}$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=f(3x).$

![](images/30/3027f0943e238d63996c8d1ff36d36b14bb60c18957168f7e54bb0a7ddcd9d33.png)

  

- Then, translate it left by $2$ units to get the graph of $y=f(3(x+2)).$

"question-2595de8f-014d-5db6-a5d3-e22363b7564e" :question/id #uuid "2595de8f-014d-5db6-a5d3-e22363b7564e" :question/math-academy-id "q-152903" :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[9X+4].$

$$
f(x)=\frac{x}{2},\,0<x<2
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[9X+4]=9\text{E}[X]+4
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[9X+4] & =9\text{E}[X]+4 \\  & =9\cdot \frac{4}{3}+4 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d5917ecc-743e-5b98-928c-b4e265150550"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-91775cc6-b3ff-5403-8a6d-5a5294e1af4c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078202 :question/problem "The first term of a geometric sequence is $2$, and the common ratio is $3.$ What is the $9$th term?" :question/worked-solution "The first term is $a_1=2,$ and the common ratio is $r=3,$ so we can write the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the $9$th term, we can use this formula with $n={\color{blue}9}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =2\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{9} & =2\cdot {3}^{9-1} \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{8} \\  & =2\cdot 6561 \\  & =13\,122\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $9$th term is $a_{9}=13\,122.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078559 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1bbae00a-a76f-5b1d-a767-0acf7498bde8" "question-18bc1e21-0c4b-52f3-824f-e719cd86e034"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078204 :question/problem "Find the formula for the $n$th term of a sequence if the $6$th term is $80$ and the common ratio is $-2.$" :question/worked-solution "The common ratio is $r=-2,$ so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & ={a}_{1}\cdot (-2)^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we still need to figure out the first term $a_1.$ We know that the $6$th term is $a_6=80,$ so we can solve for the first term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{6} & ={a}_{1}\cdot (-2)^{6-1} \\ 80 & ={a}_{1}\cdot (-2)^{5} \\ 80 & ={a}_{1}\cdot (-32) \\ -\frac{80}{32} & ={a}_{1} \\ -\frac{5}{2} & ={a}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the first term is $a_1=-\dfrac{5}{2},$ we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot (-2)^{n-1} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\cdot (-2)^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify a bit further by manipulating the exponents, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{5}{2}(-2)^{n-1} \\  & =5\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (-2)^{n-1} \\  & =5\cdot (-2)^{-1}\cdot (-2)^{n-1} \\  & =5\cdot (-2)^{n-2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078560 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-cb4d13f6-05f0-58f1-8216-e5e0e82521cb" "question-b5f78cff-3c2d-5ff5-b715-c8fb25e53460"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078203 :question/problem "Given that the $5$th term of a geometric sequence is $9$, and the common ratio is $3,$ find the second term." :question/worked-solution "The common ratio is $r=3,$ so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we still need to figure out the first term $a_1.$ We know that the $5$th term is $a_5=9,$ so we can solve for the first term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{5} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{5-1} \\ 9 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{4} \\ 9 & ={a}_{1}\cdot 81 \\ \frac{9}{81} & ={a}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{9} & ={a}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the first term is $a_1=\dfrac{1}{9},$ we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot {3}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can use this formula to compute the second term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot {3}^{2-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}

$$
a_n = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1},
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

To illustrate how this works, suppose we want to find the $10$th term of the following geometric sequence:

$$
3, \: 6, \: 12, \: \ldots
$$

The first term is $a_1=3,$ and the common ratio is $r=2,$ so we can write the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the $10$th term, we can use this formula with $n={\color{blue}10}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =3\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{10} & =3\cdot {2}^{10-1} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{9} \\  & =3\cdot 512 \\  & =1\,536\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $10$th term is $a_{10}=1\,536.$ Using the formula was much quicker than writing out all $10$ terms of the sequence!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078695 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "activity-cf46feab-8506-5fda-a24b-7fe0f9c9a46f" :activity/id #uuid "cf46feab-8506-5fda-a24b-7fe0f9c9a46f" :activity/title "Vertical Reflections of Exponential Functions" :activity/type :activity.type/review :activity/scope 17592186050955 :activity/course 17592186046647 :activity/steps ["step-10efb764-7a3b-560a-abec-d1eb97b24544" "step-1f1395c8-db59-556c-b73b-5656c71a970e" "step-04ef9537-6351-559a-927e-e766b414f4ca"] :activity/first-step "step-10efb764-7a3b-560a-abec-d1eb97b24544" :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "step-10efb764-7a3b-560a-abec-d1eb97b24544" :step/id #uuid "10efb764-7a3b-560a-abec-d1eb97b24544" :step/content 17592186115696 :step/next "step-1f1395c8-db59-556c-b73b-5656c71a970e" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-1f1395c8-db59-556c-b73b-5656c71a970e" :step/id #uuid "1f1395c8-db59-556c-b73b-5656c71a970e" :step/content 17592186299577 :step/next "step-04ef9537-6351-559a-927e-e766b414f4ca" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-04ef9537-6351-559a-927e-e766b414f4ca" :step/id #uuid "04ef9537-6351-559a-927e-e766b414f4ca" :step/content 17592186299579 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186345274 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

:question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{x}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{y}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =1-\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{1}{3}\sqrt{y} & =1-x \\ \sqrt{y} & =3(1-x) \\ (\sqrt{y})^{2} & ={(3(1-x))}^{2} \\ y & =9(1-x)^{2} \\ y & =9(x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
f^{-1}(x) = 9(x - 1)^2.
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are

$$
x \geq 0, \qquad f(x) \leq 1.
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of $f^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x \leq 1, \qquad f^{-1}(x) \geq 0.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192707 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f93430f2-f761-5264-8e7c-28207f8a2873" "question-3c4a5911-5181-51eb-9128-55f7bf7227a5" "question-0b14029b-c258-5cb1-9467-400506e4dea8"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192415 :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function ![](images/b9/b9a5eece426fa2aa66aac43b9afaf2812dcf483795a84d5e96fa89c0dcd71db6.svg)" :question/worked-solution "To find ![](images/6e/6e9ea2da83f324dd20158e4b08fb1c6968b6387d458964f21ed03648be954752.svg) we start by replacing ![](images/93/93f888a1ee0b7da5e29f442f803f1c0eaf73ad02f5eaa97e85bb8a35d607015b.svg) with ![](images/02/028bcadf67e469d96df97e89362f88bb8edca3ddea5579906987cc124663fba8.svg)

$$
y = \dfrac{1}{5}\sqrt{4x + 1}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{1}{5}\sqrt{4y + 1}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{4y+1} \\ \sqrt{4y+1} & =5x \\ {(\sqrt{4y+1})}^{2} & ={(5x)}^{2} \\ 4y+1 & =25{x}^{2} \\ 4y & =25{x}^{2}-1 \\ y & =\frac{1}{4}(25{x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(25x^2 - 1\right).
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are given by

$$
x \geq -\dfrac14, \qquad f(x) \geq 0.
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of $f^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x \geq 0, \qquad f^{-1}(x) \geq -\dfrac14.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192699 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5cb5bb60-d097-50b4-9ba5-bde88e86a4d3" "question-22e0c565-a427-5cb0-889a-a9c4e5867def" "question-635cbae5-da30-5f6f-818b-8857829587ba" "question-082ab1b4-7b0d-5301-97bc-d24a513a580b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192404 :question/problem "The function $f(x) = 3\sqrt{x + k} - 2$ has an inverse function given by $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{9}(x + 2)^2 + 3.$ What is the value of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = 3\sqrt{x+k} - 2
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = 3\sqrt{y + k} - 2.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\sqrt{y+k}-2 \\ 3\sqrt{y+k} & =x+2 \\ \sqrt{y+k} & =\frac{1}{3}(x+2) \\ {(\sqrt{y+k})}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{3}(x+2))}^{2} \\ y+k & =\frac{1}{9}(x+2)^{2} \\ y & =\frac{1}{9}(x+2)^{2}-k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{9}(x + 2)^2 - k.
$$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that

$$
-k = 3 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad k = -3.
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are given by

$$
x \geq 3, \qquad f(x) \geq -2.
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of $f^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x \geq -2, \qquad f^{-1}(x) \geq3.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-f2fd8190-fb82-5675-b05f-057d697af7cd" :question/id #uuid "f2fd8190-fb82-5675-b05f-057d697af7cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-270776" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}-10.$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$

$$

$$
x=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{y}-10.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{y}-10 \\ \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{y} & =x+10 \\ \sqrt{y} & =\frac{3}{2}(x+10) \\ (\sqrt{y})^{2} & ={(\frac{3}{2}(x+10))}^{2} \\ y & =\frac{9}{4}(x+10)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{9}{4}(x+10)^{2}.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=6-4\sqrt{x}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=6-4\sqrt{y}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6-4\sqrt{y} \\ 4\sqrt{y} & =6-x \\ \sqrt{y} & =\frac{1}{4}(6-x) \\ (\sqrt{y})^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{4}(6-x))}^{2} \\ y & =\frac{1}{16}(6-x)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{16}(6-x)^{2}.
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are

$$
x\ge 0,\,f(x)\le 6.
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of ${f}^{-1}(x)$ are

For example, let's consider the following radical function:

$$
f(x) = 3\sqrt{x} + 2
$$

To compute the inverse of $f(x),$ we follow the usual four steps:

**Step 1:** First, we replace $f(x)$ with $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
y = 3\sqrt{x} + 2
$$

**Step 2:** Then, we swap $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
x = 3\sqrt{y} + 2
$$

**Step 3:** Next, we solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\sqrt{y}+2 \\ 3\sqrt{y} & =x-2 \\ \sqrt{y} & =\frac{1}{3}(x-2) \\ (\sqrt{y})^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{3}(x-2))}^{2} \\ y & =\frac{1}{9}(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4:** Finally, we replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{9}(x - 2)^2
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are

$$
x \geq 0, \qquad f(x) \geq 2.
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of $f^{-1}(x)$ are

:question/math-academy-id "q-22308" :question/problem "If $\frac{{y}^{2}\cdot {y}^{13}}{{y}^{12}}={y}^{n},$ then $n=$" :question/worked-solution "We start by using the product rule in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}\cdot {y}^{13}}{{y}^{12}} & ={y}^{n} \\ \frac{{y}^{2+13}}{{y}^{12}} & ={y}^{n} \\ \frac{{y}^{15}}{{y}^{12}} & ={y}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{15}}{{y}^{12}} & ={y}^{n} \\ {y}^{15+(-12)} & ={y}^{n} \\ {y}^{3} & ={y}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since both sides of the equation share the same base ($y$), we can equate the exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3} & ={y}^{n} \\ 3 & =n\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $n=3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6938548d-d593-5818-8e31-5db0d3b2686a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,9{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+16{x}_{2}^{2}-50{x}_{1}+25{x}_{2}=0.
$$

 

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=9{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+16{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $25{y}_{1}^{2}$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{9{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+16{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}-50{x}_{1}+25{x}_{2}=0
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{1}+1)^{2} & ={y}_{2}+1 \\ {z}_{1}^{2} & ={z}_{2}\end{aligned}

"The disjoint union ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔{A}_{3}⊔{A}_{4}$ of events ${A}_{1},{A}_{2},{A}_{3},{A}_{4}$ covers the entire sample space. Compute $P({A}_{2}|B)$ given the following probabilities:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P(B|{A}_{1})=0.25, & P({A}_{1})=0.28 \\  & P(B|{A}_{2})=0.3, &  \\  & P(B|{A}_{3})=0.28, & P({A}_{3})=0.18 \\  & P(B|{A}_{4})=0.1, & P({A}_{4})=0.22\end{aligned}
$$

Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "If the disjoint union ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔…⊔{A}_{n}$ covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

$$
P({A}_{k}|B)=\frac{P(B|{A}_{k})P({A}_{k})}{P(B)}=\frac{P(B|{A}_{k})P({A}_{k})}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}P(B|{A}_{i})P({A}_{i})}
$$

where $k=1,2,…,n.$

In our case, $n=4,$ and ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔{A}_{3}⊔{A}_{4}$ covers the entire sample space. Consequently, we have

$$
P({A}_{1})+P({A}_{2})+P({A}_{3})+P({A}_{4})=1.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}_{2}) & =1-(P({A}_{1})+P({A}_{3})+P({A}_{4})) \\  & =1-(0.28+0.18+0.22) \\  & =0.32.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}_{2}|B) & =\frac{P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}P(B|{A}_{i})P({A}_{i})} \\  & =\frac{P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})}{P(B|{A}_{1})P({A}_{1})+P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})+P(B|{A}_{3})P({A}_{3})+P(B|{A}_{4})P({A}_{4})} \\  & =\frac{(0.3)(0.32)}{(0.25)(0.28)+(0.3)(0.32)+(0.28)(0.18)+(0.1)(0.22)} \\  & =\frac{0.096}{0.2384} \\  & ≈0.403.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-266b7c98-bb0c-5250-98ae-54d840c489c2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "095773d5-faca-5dcc-94ed-85e3db151ccc" :question/math-academy-id "q-148082" :question/problem "A medical center is investigating the correlation between scoliosis and sports practice in a sample of children.

- $25%$ of children in the sample don't practice sports, and $3%$ of those children have scoliosis.

- $30%$ of children in the sample practice one sport, and $2.5%$ of those children have scoliosis.

- $45%$ of children in the sample practice two sports, and $3.3%$ of those children have scoliosis.

If $52%$ of children in the entire sample are female, and $2%$ of female children have scoliosis, what is the probability that a randomly chosen child with scoliosis is female? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $F$ be the event that a child is female, $C$ be the event that a child has scoliosis, and ${S}_{0},{S}_{1},{S}_{2}$ be the event that a child practice $0,$ $1,$ or $2$ sports, respectively.

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({S}_{0})=0.25 &  & P(C|{S}_{0})=0.03 \\  & P({S}_{1})=0.30 &  & P(C|{S}_{1})=0.025 \\  & P({S}_{2})=0.45 &  & P(C|{S}_{2})=0.033\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${S}_{0}⊔{S}_{1}⊔{S}_{2}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$

of children.

- $25%$ of children in the sample don't practice sports, and $2.5%$ of those children have scoliosis.

- $30%$ of children in the sample practice one sport.

Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $F$ be the event that a child is female, $C$ be the event that a child has scoliosis, and ${S}_{0},{S}_{1},{S}_{2}$ be the event that a child practices $0,$ $1,$ or $2$ sports, respectively.

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({S}_{0})=0.25 &  & P(C∣{S}_{0})=0.025 \\  & P({S}_{1})=0.30 \\  & P({S}_{2})=0.45 &  & P(C∣{S}_{2})=0.028\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${S}_{0}⊔{S}_{1}⊔{S}_{2}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({S}_{0})+P({S}_{1})+P({S}_{2})=0.25+0.30+0.45=1.
$$

- Since $48%$ of students in the entire sample are female, we have

$$
P(F)=0.48.
$$

- Since $2.6%$ of females have scoliosis, we have

$$
P(C∣F)=0.026.
$$

- Since $46%$ of children with scoliosis are female, we have

$$
P(F∣C)=0.46.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen child who practices one sport has scoliosis, which is represented as $P(C∣{S}_{1}).$

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(F∣C) & =\frac{P(C∣F)P(F)}{P(C)} \\ P(F∣C) & =\frac{P(C∣F)P(F)}{P(C∣{S}_{0})P({S}_{0})+P(C∣{S}_{1})P({S}_{1})+P(C∣{S}_{2})P({S}_{2})} \\ 0.46 & =\frac{(0.026)(0.48)}{(0.25)(0.025)+P(C∣{S}_{1})(0.3)+(0.028)(0.45)} \\ 0.46 & =\frac{0.0125}{0.0189+0.3P(C∣{S}_{1})}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(C∣{S}_{1}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.46(0.0189+0.3P(C∣{S}_{1})) & =0.0125 \\ 0.0189+0.3P(C∣{S}_{1}) & =\frac{0.0125}{0.46} \\ 0.3P(C∣{S}_{1}) & =\frac{0.0125}{0.46}-0.0189 \\ P(C∣{S}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{0.3}(\frac{0.0125}{0.46}-0.0189) \\ P(C∣{S}_{1}) & ≈0.028\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2d9e6faf-9e8f-5d9c-aa84-79845b127ed4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 3}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b),$ where

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 10 \\ 20\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 8\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]?$

<table cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="70px" rowspan="2" width="30px">

</td>
<td align="center" height="35px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-2}}</td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="35px"></td>
<td align="center">$0$</td>
<td align="center">{{field-4}}</td>
<td align="center">$-160$</td>

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)=y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}={y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{3}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 10 \\ 20\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 8\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 10 & 20\end{aligned}] \\  & =([\begin{aligned}20 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 8\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 10 & 20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 \\ -8\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 10 & 20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 130 & 260 \\ 0 & -80 & -160\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203428 :answer-field/correct "answer-390d31e7-0eb4-5afa-8052-7ccdd44c6579" :answer-field/choices "078844cb-65ac-54f4-bde7-64e4bd44f313" :question/math-academy-id "q-269466" :question/problem "Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 2}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=2(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b),$ where

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 10\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]?$

<table cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="70px" rowspan="2" width="30px">

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)=2{y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}(2{y}^{T}y)=4y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=4{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i}.
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =4{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =4{y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $4$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x,$ so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=4y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =4y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}10 \\ 10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =4([\begin{aligned}20 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}76 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}760 & 760 \\ -40 & -40\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-86a09f03-3f8a-5c3f-9183-dbfb9af6dd2a" "answer-field-a107a0f3-3d37-50c0-a77a-33925b86f16a"] :db/ensure Therefore, the domain of $g(x)$ is $x\in(-\infty,\infty).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124584 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0bc8d353-4f35-531e-9326-d4dcbc01bbdb" "question-9acd8689-6770-5d1b-9670-f2ff78d7e31a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124393 :question/problem "What is the range of the function $f(x) = (x+3)^2-2?$" :question/worked-solution "The parabola is written in vertex form, 

$$
y = a(x-h)^2 + k,
$$

where $a$ is the leading coefficient and $(h,k)$ is the vertex. 

- Since $h=-3$ and $k=-2,$ the vertex is $(-3,-2).$

- Since $a=1>0,$ the parabola opens upwards.

Because the parabola opens upwards, the vertex corresponds to the minimum output, while there is no maximum output. 

Therefore, the range is $[-2,\infty).$

The corresponding diagram is shown below.

![](images/57/579eef7814c2b51c44cded6fb2dc64e36d1106d359864e1e7ec7354511f80681.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124659 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c749b226-6df0-583d-9d39-da82636ab3b6" "question-0eda0ab3-fc3e-57ae-8050-823c01afb804" "question-7dfd6f87-7029-50ed-aece-aeae8cb98e8c" "question-28ef6032-c464-5039-b5ee-d8d9a6314099"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124225 :question/problem "What is the range of the function $f(x)=x^2+4x+6?$" :question/worked-solution "The given parabola is written in standard form,

$$
y = ax^2+bx+c,
$$

with $a=1>0,$ $b=4,$ and $c=6.$

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the parabola opens upward. Consequently, there is no maximum output, and the vertex corresponds to the minimum output.

The $x$-coordinate of the vertex is given by

$$
x= -\dfrac{b}{2a} = -\dfrac{4}{2 \cdot 1} = -2.
$$

Now, we substitute $x=-2$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{2}+4x+6 \\  & =(-2)^{2}+4(-2)+6 \\  & =4-8+6 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(-2,2),$ and the range of the function is $[2,\infty).$

![](images/41/41b7219793120c0e37b3d910ef6a8f3754c1d9f27b784f937381743d7b7a85df.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124660 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0dff1477-477e-5350-b60a-a888d8f2c5e5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124226 :question/problem "What is the range of the function $f(x) = -\dfrac{1}{2}(x+3)(x-1)?$" :question/worked-solution "The given parabola is written in factored form,

$$
y = a(x-x_1)(x-x_2),
$$

with $a = -\dfrac{1}{2} <    0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are $x_1=-3$ and $x_2=1,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-3+1}{2}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=-1$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}(x+3)(x-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-1+3)(-1-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot (-2) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(-1,2),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty,2].$

$$
y=a(x-h)^{2}+k,
$$

- Since $a=1>0,$ the parabola opens upwards.

Because the parabola opens upwards, there is no maximum output, and the vertex corresponds to the minimum output. 

Therefore, the range is $[-3,\infty ).$

$$
y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c,
$$

with $a=1>0,$ $b=0,$ and $c=1.$

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the parabola opens upward. Consequently, there is no maximum output, and the vertex corresponds to the minimum output.

The $x$-coordinate of the vertex is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac{0}{2\cdot 1}=0.
$$

Now, we substitute $x=0$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{2}+1 \\  & =(0)^{2}+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(0,1),$ and the range of the function is $[1,\infty ).$

$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(-2,-5),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,-5].$

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-\frac{1}{3}<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=2,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-2+2}{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=0$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x+2)(x-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(0+2)(0-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(0,\frac{4}{3}),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,\frac{4}{3}].$

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-2<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=3,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-1+3}{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=1$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2(x+1)(x-3) \\  & =-2(1+1)(1-3) \\  & =-2\cdot 2\cdot (-2) \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(1,8),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,8],$ i.e. $-\infty <f(x)\le 8.$

17592186125716 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will discuss the properties of quadratic functions. Specifically, we learn how to determine the domain and range of a quadratic function.

Remember that a quadratic function takes the form

$$
f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c,
$$

where $a,b,$ and $c$ are constants.

The first thing to note is that the domain of *any* quadratic function is $x\in (-\infty, \infty)$ because it is defined for all values of $x.$

Determining the range of a quadratic function is slightly more involved, as we'll see shortly." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125846 :tutorial/content "The range of a quadratic function depends on the direction in which its graph opens. Regardless of whether the equation is written in standard form,

$$
y = ax^2 + bx + c,
$$

vertex form, 

$$
y = a(x-h)^2 + k,
$$

or factored form,

$$
y = a(x-x_1)(x-x_2),
$$

it opens upwards if the leading coefficient $a$ is positive and downwards if $a$ is negative.

Now, consider a parabola that opens upwards ($a>0$). In this case, the minimum output corresponds to the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, while there is no maximum output. Therefore, if the vertex is $(h,k),$ then the range is $y \geq k.$

For example, in the graph below, the $y$-value of the vertex is $y=-2$, so the range of the function is $y \geq -2.$

In this case, there is no minimum output, but the maximum output corresponds to the $y$-coordinate of the vertex. Therefore, if the vertex is $(h,k),$ then the range is $y \leq k.$

For example, in the graph below, the $y$-value of the vertex is $y=2$, so the range of the function is $y \leq 2.$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡({{field-1}})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡({{field-2}}).
$$

The $7$th sine coefficient of the series is

$$
{b}_{7}={{field-3}}.
$$

Given that $F(x)=x$ and $L=2\pi ,$ the $7$th sine coefficient becomes

$$
{b}_{7}={{field-4}}\,\cdot \,{{field-5}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k\ne 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\frac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)
$$

must have a period of $2L\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}=2\pi .$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)
$$

Therefore, $7$th sine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{7} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(7s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(7s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=2\pi $ and $f(x)=x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{7} & =\frac{1}{2\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{2\pi }x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7}{2}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-805880d3-7d18-5740-8087-2ae8c15c331c" "answer-field-1ef4925b-0108-5329-895d-9d6319c347a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-341777" :question/problem "Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in [-L,L)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡({{field-1}})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡({{field-2}}).
$$

The $6$th cosine coefficient of the series is

$$
{a}_{6}={{field-3}}.
$$

Given that $F(x)={e}^{-{x}^{2}}$ and $L=5,$ the $6$th cosine coefficient becomes

$$
{a}_{6}={{field-4}}\,\cdot \,{{field-5}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k\ne 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\frac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)
$$

must have a period of $2L\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}=2\pi .$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)
$$

Therefore, $6$th cosine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{6} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(6s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(6s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=5$ and $f(x)={e}^{-{x}^{2}},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{6} & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot {\int }_{-5}^{5}{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{5}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-91327f8b-24a5-5a14-b72f-dc506b7dc1e0" "answer-field-27849c49-d7ae-5d00-af0d-9052f43cd943" f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{2}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{2}x)

Let $F(x)=-3x+3$ for $x\in [-2,2).$ The Fourier series of the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and $f(x)=-3x+3$ for $x\in [-2,2).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(-3x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+3x]}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((-\frac{3}{2}\cdot {2}^{2}+3\cdot 2)-(-\frac{3}{2}\cdot (-2)^{2}+3\cdot (-2))) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(0-(-12)) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b3e4d068-52a7-54b2-9f52-ab0c0b143b6e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b3e4d068-52a7-54b2-9f52-ab0c0b143b6e" :answer-field/id #uuid "b3e4d068-52a7-54b2-9f52-ab0c0b143b6e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-1f47cc34-1a40-54f8-8f21-1937b1207c8c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1f47cc34-1a40-54f8-8f21-1937b1207c8c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1f47cc34-1a40-54f8-8f21-1937b1207c8c" :answer/id #uuid "1f47cc34-1a40-54f8-8f21-1937b1207c8c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-14280c74-af6e-5d18-9712-69501b60ddc5" :question/id #uuid "14280c74-af6e-5d18-9712-69501b60ddc5" :question/math-academy-id "q-341830" :question/problem "$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n}{2}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n}{2}x)

The Fourier series of the $4\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function

$$

is shown above. Find the exact value of ${b}_{3}.$

${b}_{3}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the sine coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2\pi .$ Also, $f(x)=5$ for $x\in [0,2\pi )$ and $f(x)=-2$ for $x\in [-2\pi ,0).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2\pi }{\int }_{-2\pi }^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3}{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }{\int }_{-2\pi }^{0}(-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3}{2}x)\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3}{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{2}{2\pi }\cdot (-\frac{2}{3}){[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3}{2}x)]}_{-2\pi }^{0}+\frac{5}{2\pi }\cdot (-\frac{2}{3}){[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3}{2}x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{3\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3\pi ))-\frac{5}{3\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{2}{3\pi }(1-(-1))-\frac{5}{3\pi }((-1)-1) \\  & =\frac{4}{3\pi }+\frac{10}{3\pi } \\  & =\frac{14}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-50ebbed4-eb9c-5659-8b8c-f37f72666390"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-50ebbed4-eb9c-5659-8b8c-f37f72666390" :answer-field/id #uuid "50ebbed4-eb9c-5659-8b8c-f37f72666390" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f308dd20-f66e-5ffb-861b-4ab8333e47b2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f308dd20-f66e-5ffb-861b-4ab8333e47b2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f308dd20-f66e-5ffb-861b-4ab8333e47b2" :answer/id #uuid "f308dd20-f66e-5ffb-861b-4ab8333e47b2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{14}{3\pi}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e5dc675f-f1b9-58e9-a567-64d8cd60aaaf" :question/id #uuid "e5dc675f-f1b9-58e9-a567-64d8cd60aaaf" :question/math-academy-id "q-341873" :question/problem "$$

Let $F(x)=2x+7$ for $x\in [-3,3).$ The Fourier series of the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${a}_{1}.$

${a}_{1}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=3$ and $f(x)=2x+7$ for $x\in [-3,3).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(2x+7)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x+7\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{3}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}(uv\,{|}_{-3}^{3}-{\int }_{-3}^{3}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{3}{\pi }{[(2x+7)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{3}-{\int }_{-3}^{3}\frac{3}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)\cdot 2\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{3}{\pi }[13\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )]-\frac{6}{\pi }{\int }_{-3}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{3}{\pi }\cdot 0-\frac{6}{\pi }\cdot (-\frac{3}{\pi }){[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{18}{{\pi }^{2}}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )]) \\  & =\frac{6}{{\pi }^{2}}(-1-(-1)) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2afc926f-9cf1-5b4f-8748-f140b3012b4a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2afc926f-9cf1-5b4f-8748-f140b3012b4a" :answer-field/id #uuid "2afc926f-9cf1-5b4f-8748-f140b3012b4a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-96e025f6-a797-5f53-bd93-ef33e6a27f03" :answer-field/choices ["answer-96e025f6-a797-5f53-bd93-ef33e6a27f03"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-96e025f6-a797-5f53-bd93-ef33e6a27f03" :answer/id #uuid "96e025f6-a797-5f53-bd93-ef33e6a27f03" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8c3f231c-8d0c-511e-b4f9-0d81c5e6659f" :question/id #uuid "8c3f231c-8d0c-511e-b4f9-0d81c5e6659f" :question/math-academy-id "q-341863" :question/problem "$$

${a}_{2}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and $f(x)=x+1$ for $x\in [-2,2).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x+1\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(uv\,{|}_{-2}^{2}-{\int }_{-2}^{2}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{\pi }{[(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)]}_{-2}^{2}-{\int }_{-2}^{2}\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{\pi }[3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-(-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )]-\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot (-\frac{1}{\pi }){[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)]}_{-2}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot 0+\frac{1}{{\pi }^{2}}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2\pi )]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{\pi }^{2}}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a7ebfbb0-eafe-5de9-be9a-5eb3748e9483"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a7ebfbb0-eafe-5de9-be9a-5eb3748e9483" :answer-field/id #uuid "a7ebfbb0-eafe-5de9-be9a-5eb3748e9483" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-88ed5bbc-d47f-5994-8b20-ac726fec6a85" :answer-field/choices ["answer-88ed5bbc-d47f-5994-8b20-ac726fec6a85"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-88ed5bbc-d47f-5994-8b20-ac726fec6a85" :answer/id #uuid "88ed5bbc-d47f-5994-8b20-ac726fec6a85" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-46598e7e-81d3-578b-80cc-94d59f9707e8" :question/id #uuid "46598e7e-81d3-578b-80cc-94d59f9707e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-341861" :question/problem "$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-4x$ for $x\in [-\pi ,\pi ).$ The Fourier series of the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${b}_{2}.$

${b}_{2}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the sine coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=\pi $ and $f(x)=-4x$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(-4x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{\pi }x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(-4x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-4x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-4 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi }-{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{2}{[(-4x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)]}_{-\pi }^{\pi }-{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))(-4)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{2}((-4\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-(4\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2\pi ))-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{2}((-4\pi )\cdot 1-(4\pi )\cdot 1)-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)]}_{-\pi }^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }(4\pi -(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot (4\pi -0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6c30a88d-8e13-5d71-9185-007060f3d4e5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6c30a88d-8e13-5d71-9185-007060f3d4e5" :answer-field/id #uuid "6c30a88d-8e13-5d71-9185-007060f3d4e5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-824395f4-e1d3-5e0f-879c-0d03e310d7a5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-824395f4-e1d3-5e0f-879c-0d03e310d7a5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-824395f4-e1d3-5e0f-879c-0d03e310d7a5" :answer/id #uuid "824395f4-e1d3-5e0f-879c-0d03e310d7a5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124552 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a0915342-2d27-50ea-9893-ae57d8dcc177"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-a0915342-2d27-50ea-9893-ae57d8dcc177" :question/id #uuid "a0915342-2d27-50ea-9893-ae57d8dcc177" :question/math-academy-id "q-83392" :question/problem "Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}-23 & -15 \\ 9 & 19\end{aligned}],$ find the sum of the eigenvalues of $A.$" :question/worked-solution "The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the sum of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the trace of $A.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A)=-23+19=-4.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c74d7ddb-fc22-5cce-9d10-5c29a729de7c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c74d7ddb-fc22-5cce-9d10-5c29a729de7c" :answer-field/id #uuid "c74d7ddb-fc22-5cce-9d10-5c29a729de7c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4c890fb7-5ad0-51ee-b262-8eccfdca2316" :answer-field/choices ["answer-29518f7d-c336-5d57-8db0-9a4b5ee70722" "answer-4c890fb7-5ad0-51ee-b262-8eccfdca2316" "answer-c15f40ae-67d9-59f5-916f-7f95aad7031a" "answer-de4777f6-8208-5517-8ce8-3d1cffc8e9b6" "answer-dde652cb-50a6-5b2b-a8b3-f6fce0861332"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-29518f7d-c336-5d57-8db0-9a4b5ee70722" :answer/id #uuid "29518f7d-c336-5d57-8db0-9a4b5ee70722" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4c890fb7-5ad0-51ee-b262-8eccfdca2316" :answer/id #uuid "4c890fb7-5ad0-51ee-b262-8eccfdca2316" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c15f40ae-67d9-59f5-916f-7f95aad7031a" :answer/id #uuid "c15f40ae-67d9-59f5-916f-7f95aad7031a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-de4777f6-8208-5517-8ce8-3d1cffc8e9b6" :answer/id #uuid "de4777f6-8208-5517-8ce8-3d1cffc8e9b6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "42" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dde652cb-50a6-5b2b-a8b3-f6fce0861332" :answer/id #uuid "dde652cb-50a6-5b2b-a8b3-f6fce0861332" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125824 :tutorial/content "If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](images/0f/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078570 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-470997c7-250a-5a72-adc9-b7b406031a9e" "question-2ac819b8-8252-5f38-81b6-27fb48d49f54"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-470997c7-250a-5a72-adc9-b7b406031a9e" :question/id #uuid "470997c7-250a-5a72-adc9-b7b406031a9e" :question/math-academy-id "q-5338" :question/problem "Evaluate ${\sum }_{n=1}^{3}5\cdot {2}^{n-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "The sum takes integer values of $n$ from $1$ to $3.$ So, computing the terms for $n=1,2,3$ and then adding them, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{3}5\cdot {2}^{n-1} & =(5\cdot {2}^{1-1})+(5\cdot {2}^{2-1})+(5\cdot {2}^{3-1}) \\  & =(5\cdot {2}^{0})+(5\cdot {2}^{1})+(5\cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & =(5\cdot 1)+(5\cdot 2)+(5\cdot 4) \\  & =5+10+20 \\  & =35.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fba6865d-0f42-54a0-ae09-88d638e07043"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "dd5db24a-0334-5fd9-a195-a6f3785eda3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-66995" :question/problem "Express $S=8+16+24+⋯+80+88$ in sigma notation." :question/worked-solution "Notice that the terms of the corresponding sequence

$$
8,\,16,\,24,\,…,\,80,\,88.
$$

 are multiples of $8,$ and since $88÷8=11,$ there are $11$ terms in total. 

Therefore, the $n$th term of the sequence has the form

$$
{a}_{n}=8n,
$$

where $n$ ranges from $n=1$ to $n=11.$ Indeed: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =8(1)=8 \\ {a}_{2} & =8(2)=16 \\ {a}_{3} & =8(3)=24 \\  & \,\,⋮ \\ {a}_{10} & =8(10)=80 \\ {a}_{11} & =8(11)=88\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S=8+16+24+⋯+80+88={\sum }_{n=1}^{11}8n.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-944f2e05-631f-5917-979a-ad00e83fe8a8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "0f78e83e-c080-5c56-8a40-9938a1632481" :question/math-academy-id "q-345102" :question/problem "A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $9\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $45\,Ω,$ a capacitance of $0.01\,\text{F},$ and an inductance of $L=15\,\text{H}.$ Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds).

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "We have the following circuit diagram.

![](images/34/34ed425a41460e1fca35a028c2bd7add953d0b354b28a4d4f2ab02bab67a78a8.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=45\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=45I=45\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.01}=100q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=15\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=15\,\frac{dI}{dt}=15\,\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dq}{dt})=15\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
9=45\,\frac{dq}{dt}+100q+15\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+3\,\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{20}{3}q=\frac{3}{5}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7715413d-38fa-550a-b8f7-7de3c69db2ed"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id
