$t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ for the curve $r(t)=⟨t,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨1,-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨0,-{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ and ${r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-2,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-2\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖} \\  & =\frac{(\sqrt{2})^{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186266138 :question/id #uuid "662600c1-093e-5a2d-9c1b-c63b30fbe5ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-132125"} {:db/id 17592186266139 :question/id #uuid "fc98fe78-7bbc-5b33-b834-f98e5a5a6e2e" :question/math-academy-id "q-132128"} {:db/id 17592186266140 :question/id #uuid "7d2943df-d322-57f9-9465-3be5dfbf7067" :question/math-academy-id "q-132129" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18e7b0c5-59c8-5276-8f27-e519196c22e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2}" :db/id 17592186263236} {:answer/id #uuid "5c697a54-9e06-52cc-9c8e-9e93cd4a2158" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}{e}^{\pi }}{2}" :db/id 17592186263796} {:answer/id #uuid "a532f5f7-12c2-5842-a3e6-eb768839607c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2}" :db/id 17592186264413} {:answer/id #uuid "ab6b8756-6f83-5bd9-aa3b-ae5978576099" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{\pi }" :db/id 17592186264473} {:answer/id #uuid "bb8a8631-251a-5a00-aa65-16be619ec141" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}{e}^{-\pi }" :db/id 17592186264630}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264630} :answer-field/id #uuid "805bbad1-9820-5da9-8726-919fd6256468" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265470}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=\pi $ for the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-t}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-t}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\times 2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖} \\  & =\frac{({e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2})^{3}}{2{e}^{-2\pi }} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}{e}^{-3\pi }}{2{e}^{-2\pi }} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{-\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186266141 :question/id #uuid "cf0c275d-135e-528b-bd00-cb3abdf966eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-132130"} {:db/id 17592186320790 :question/id #uuid "f89d804c-5610-5e9d-94e2-86a0ad458afd" :question/math-academy-id "q-35114"} {:db/id 17592186362307 :question/id #uuid "61a53a3d-9f1a-5b06-bcde-4575632a0617" :question/math-academy-id "q-98665" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bfef024-1b6c-555f-8a26-33bf987ce229" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186360947} {:answer/id #uuid "5b8d1fdb-1e8d-5f02-9ea7-c3c298ae432f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{4}" :db/id 17592186361248} {:answer/id #uuid "af862e42-0cba-5667-86e1-bcba2137990c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186361614} {:answer/id #uuid "c253a7fe-6f5f-512c-aff1-bf5aa8dd058e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186361708} {:answer/id #uuid "ed37a445-de09-58c0-b587-33b13984c10f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186361889}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186360947} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf9e95f8-2048-5fb9-b5b3-a7a136bdb4eb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362172}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ for the curve $r(t)=⟨{cos}^{3}⁡t,{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t),$ ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{3}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{3}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,3{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨-3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})⟩ \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨-1,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{3}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t-3{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}){sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-3{cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-3{sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨6(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}){(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}-3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{3},6(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}){(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}-3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ and ${r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩\times (\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & ={(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})}^{2}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \,-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}\,-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{8}\cdot 2\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{4}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}=\frac{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{3}}{\,\frac{9}{4}\,}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362308 :question/id #uuid "a52b4e8f-8a80-5361-a7aa-97f65400f662" :question/math-academy-id "q-98668"} {:db/id 17592186362317 :question/id #uuid "5692f221-3e0b-5059-a8e0-07dee6b9fc2a" :question/math-academy-id "q-98708"} {:db/id 17592186444695 :question/id #uuid "577c86ab-d1fb-551c-9998-1ea74c39e37e" :question/math-academy-id "q-132119"} {:db/id 17592186444697 :question/id #uuid "8e82dd54-dc76-5073-8b6d-fd7d44dc815e" :question/math-academy-id "q-98717"} {:db/id 17592186478445 :question/id #uuid "bee1b915-a838-5542-8a64-106e980bc53d" :question/math-academy-id "q-98666" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3ea7b209-5616-55d5-9904-552d1c0715cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186477851} {:answer/id #uuid "5ff08d81-960b-574d-bb5a-4735a65941c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186477931} {:answer/id #uuid "623c10d1-ccda-5676-a53a-28fffcd4fe76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186477937} {:answer/id #uuid "6d62eea6-536d-5d3a-b711-a9c0a42702d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186477961} {:answer/id #uuid "729b116e-a1cd-54d1-af16-82f64c0e08d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186477977}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186477851} :answer-field/id #uuid "3901cec7-c587-5a5c-8a5e-3e53db5169e0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186478270}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=1$ for the curve $r(t)=⟨t,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t),$ ${r}^{′}(1)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\frac{1}{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(1)$ and ${r}^{″}(1)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨1,1,0⟩\times ⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & \,\,-1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, the radius of the osculating circle at  $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}=\frac{(\sqrt{2})^{3}}{\,1\,}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$
B=\{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\},\,[T]_{B|C}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ (shown above) and a basis $C$ of ${R}^{3}.$
The matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the linear map $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{3}$ relative to these bases, and the vector $x\in {R}^{2},$ are also given. Find $[T(x)]_{C}.$" :question/worked-solution "We can find the coordinates of the image of $x$ under $T$ relative to the basis $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $[x]_{B},$ the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B.$ So, let

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This gives us the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1} &=-4 \\ -2{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=-3.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We now row-reduce the corresponding augmented matrix using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & -4 \\ -2 & 5 & -3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 4 \\ -2 & 5 & -3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 & 5\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 5 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ are the bases of the vector spaces $V$ and $W$, respectively. Find the matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the map $T$ relative to these bases, if 

$\,$ $T({b}_{1})=-3{c}_{1}-5{c}_{2},\,$ $T({b}_{2})={c}_{1}-4{c}_{2}\,$ and $\,T({b}_{3})=5{c}_{1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the images of vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}T({b}_{1})=-3{c}_{1}-5{c}_{2} & \,⟹\,[T({b}_{1})]_{C}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\ T({b}_{2})={c}_{1}-4{c}_{2} & \,⟹\,[T({b}_{2})]_{C}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ T({b}_{3})=5{c}_{1} & \,⟹\,[T({b}_{3})]_{C}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $[T]_{B|C}$ is the matrix  whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2})$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
[T]_{B|C}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 & 5 \\ -5 & -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124604 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124416 :question/id #uuid "3d6b0aec-c282-581e-ae4a-560654d80e3b" :question/math-academy-id "e-8605"} :knowledge-point/id {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the basis $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ of the vector space $V$ and the basis $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ given by

$$
C=\{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\}.
$$

Find the matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the map $T:V\to {R}^{2}$ relative to these bases if 

$$
T({b}_{1})=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,T({b}_{2})=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $[T]_{B|C}$ is the matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $C.$

First, we need to find the coordinates of $T({b}_{i})$ relative to the basis $C$ for each $i=1,2.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the following matrix:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) \\ | & | & | & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 9 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the right-hand side gives the matrix of the linear transformation relative to the bases $B$ and $C:$

$$
[T]_{B|C}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050820 :topic/difficulty 0.640892872444543 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428522 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. :db/id 17592186127129}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find an eigenvector of $A=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 9 & -7 \\ -14 & 13 & -8 \\ -2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 9 & -7 \\ -14 & 13 & -8 \\ -2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 9 & -7 \\ -14 & 10 & -8 \\ -2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-12{x}_{1}+9{x}_{2}-7{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -14{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 9 & -7 & 0 \\ -14 & 10 & -8 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -14 & 10 & -8 & 0 \\ -12 & 9 & -7 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-7){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{2}(-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-(\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3})+{x}_{3}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=3,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$"} {:db/id 17592186129609 :question/id #uuid "21a6142d-2e2d-5db8-9f67-5431e9644165" :question/math-academy-id "q-37405"} {:db/id 17592186272147 :question/id #uuid "00737dc0-f397-573a-80e1-d038ce87150d" :question/math-academy-id "q-140717" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3279f5ec-b5ad-574c-aebf-693bd2fdaa1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186269730} {:answer/id #uuid "653c963e-8cbf-558c-a076-0707a4bd7a0e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186270171} {:answer/id #uuid "7e7e2990-b7e7-5be9-a37d-ee55358620c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186270375} {:answer/id #uuid "81fcddb5-5383-56b8-bcf4-c993974f8e45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186270392} {:answer/id #uuid "ca767cd0-e2d5-5f15-b839-31ed41909f67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186271045}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186270392} :answer-field/id #uuid "87f091c3-7851-5215-bc6b-9b792d0722c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186271748}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find an eigenvector of $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -3\end{bmatrix}$

$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{2}:=(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\  & ={x}_{2}+2(0) \\  & ={x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -9{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.

$$

What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "Since $A$ is an upper triangular matrix, we have that its eigenvalues are the entries in the main diagonal, that is, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

Also, since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 7 & 2 \\ 0 & -9 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-4{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -9{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 0 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Notice that the augmented matrix $M$ is already in its row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 7 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{2}{9}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{4}(7{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(7(\frac{2}{9}{x}_{3})+2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{32}{9}{x}_{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{8}{9}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{2}{9}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=9,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 2 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-1.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-(-1)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =-2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 0 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{5}{3} & -\frac{20}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=4{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}(-2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2(4{x}_{3})-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =-4{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-4{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.

$$

Also, since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =6.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -5 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{1} &=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}-11{x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+5{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

:question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[2e-(e-1)X].$

$$
f(x)=\frac{e}{e{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}},\,1<x<e
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[2e-(e-1)X]=2e-(e-1)\text{E}[X]
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}x\cdot \frac{e}{e{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{e}{ex-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{e}{e-1}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{e}{e-1}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{e}{e-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2e-(e-1)X] & =2e-(e-1)\text{E}[X] \\  & =2e-(e-1)\cdot \frac{e}{e-1} \\  & =2e-e \\  & =e.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186436282 :question/id #uuid "c64c8376-4f9a-5df0-81b9-bf811d12f7ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-152904" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12065d32-e113-5992-bb8d-f535e75fb9ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{2}" :db/id 17592186436257} {:answer/id #uuid "18efb766-1d3d-58da-bff5-d24f02292777" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186436258} {:answer/id #uuid "29173ece-c32d-5596-a3a8-34d0349c05ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/id 17592186436259} {:answer/id #uuid "a2a8b51a-6b08-55ab-89b7-ef577ff59874" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{8}" :db/id 17592186436268} {:answer/id #uuid "b73c6eb0-be0e-57a4-8c3b-4e4f51c6378c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186436269}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186436257} :answer-field/id #uuid "76d69cbc-7ea6-5219-b9fe-b27e60e2aa63" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186436277}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[4X+2].$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}, & 0<x\le 1, \\ \frac{1}{2{x}^{3}}, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of the expected value:

$$
\text{E}[4X+2]=4\text{E}[X]+2
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{3}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }x\cdot \frac{1}{2{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3x}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{3{x}^{2}}{8})|}_{0}^{1}+{(-\frac{1}{2x})|}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =(\frac{3}{8}-0)+(0-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4X+2] & =4\text{E}[X]+2 \\  & =4\cdot \frac{7}{8}+2 \\  & =\frac{11}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186436283 :question/id #uuid "edac9b93-8284-5302-bc8b-9583d4ecc8f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-152907" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "30945d0b-c228-50cd-9399-4fc6759027b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186436260} {:answer/id #uuid "477a366f-5027-5734-8066-1c5b19a5ae4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{8}" :db/id 17592186436262} {:answer/id #uuid "52eacba8-2ac3-5a25-85fe-9c675a072c68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186436263} {:answer/id #uuid "5ffc82d5-d3b0-5643-95db-cbc049b36c70" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{9}" :db/id 17592186436264} {:answer/id #uuid "c10ec2db-f24e-557d-8a16-961d2cfcd677" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186436270}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186436260} :answer-field/id #uuid "a9112695-ad08-5300-a06c-ea0b770acb45" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186436278}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[12X-8].$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}, & 0<x\le 1, \\ \frac{8}{9}, & 1\le x<2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of the expected value:

$$
\text{E}[12X-8]=12\text{E}[X]-8
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{8}{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{8x}{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{4}}{12})|}_{0}^{1}+{\frac{4{x}^{2}}{9}|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{12}-0)+(\frac{16}{9}-\frac{4}{9}) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}+\frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{17}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[12X-8] & =12\text{E}[X]-8 \\  & =12\cdot \frac{17}{12}-8 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186192677 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192619 :question/id #uuid "3a11b9e3-60c8-57f3-8ec6-4ff378d0db62" :question/math-academy-id "e-7987"} :knowledge-point/id :topic/math-academy-id 1834} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120595 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121008 :tutorial/content "The **osculating circle** (sometimes called the *kissing circle*) of a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is a circle that

- is tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P,$ and

- has the same curvature as the curve $C$ at the point $P.$

To demonstrate, consider the curve $C$ given by the vector function

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle t+1, 2-t^2\rangle.
$$

The curve $C$ and its osculating circle at the point $P$ are shown in the diagram below.

![](images/f5/f51c1d1f45f2484991c28296d9b9ceeda134965993d130c2611c0e4bfb4ab32b.png)

At the point $P(1,2),$ where $t=0,$ the curvature is $\kappa(0)=2.$

It can be proved that any circle has constant curvature, which is equal to the reciprocal of the circle's radius. So, for a general curve $\mathbf r (t)$ we define its 
 **radius of curvature** as

$$
R(t) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (t)}. % = \dfrac{\left\|\mathbf r'(t)\right\|}{\| \mathbf T'(t) \|}
$$

In our example above, we get

$$
R(0) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (0)} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

**Watch out!** Since computing the radius of curvature requires computing the curvature first, we might use different formulas for curvature depending on the situation.

For example, if a curve is parametrized by its arc length, we use the formula

$$
R(s) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (s)} = \dfrac{1}{\| \mathbf{T}'(s) \|}.
$$

On the other hand, if a curve uses a general parameter $t,$ we use the formula

$$
R(t) = \dfrac 1 {\kappa (t)} = \dfrac{\left\|\mathbf r'(t)\right\|}{\| \mathbf T'(t) \|}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b58176ee-322d-5b4a-aa8c-e9972cbe1229" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2488 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "812b9e66-1124-5116-9356-ca760a8dde07" :step/math-academy-id 11116 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120596}} {:db/id 17592186120596 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119758 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119574 :question/id #uuid "3e36e916-16af-55eb-9ece-026b68eb93ea" :question/math-academy-id "e-3338"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4d622a24-2705-53bb-a07f-8cc11775cf09" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049196}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120322} {:db/id 17592186120353} {:db/id 17592186235465} {:db/id 17592186266134} {:db/id 17592186266135} {:db/id 17592186266136} {:db/id 17592186335739} {:db/id 17592186335740} {:db/id 17592186444696} {:db/id 17592186492052} {:db/id 17592186492066}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Radius of Curvature"} :step/id #uuid "869f0a40-96aa-5ddd-b227-5006ff45ea4d" :step/math-academy-id 11118 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120597}} {:db/id 17592186120597 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121009 :tutorial/content "The center of the osculating circle for a curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at a point where $t=t_0$ is located at the tip of the vector 

$$
\mathbf r(t_0)+R(t_0) \mathbf N(t_0)
$$

where $\mathbf N(t)$ denotes the principal normal vector to the curve.

For example, the curve $C$ parameterized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \bigg\langle t+1, 2- \dfrac{t^2}{2} \bigg\rangle
$$

has the normal vector

$$
\mathbf{N}(t) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+t^2}} \langle -t, \: -1 \rangle ,
$$

and the radius of curvature at the point $P(1,2)$ where $t=0$ is $R(0)=1.$

So, the center of the osculating circle is at the tip of the vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0+1,\,2-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}⟩+1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}}}⟨0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2⟩+⟨0,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the center of the osculating circle at the point where $t=0$ is located at $\left(1, 1 \right),$ as shown below.

![](images/d8/d8cd8407e6398b3409e7f575e152976669393914e2e5d7335121287276af6e41.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "5a31a99b-6c09-5d1c-ad68-7b5f38c17efb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2489 :tutorial/title "The Center of the Osculating Circle"} :step/id #uuid "88a27337-45d9-59ab-ac93-024d63adfb66" :step/math-academy-id 11120 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120598}} {:db/id 17592186120598 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119759 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119575 :question/id #uuid "7f4861fe-a783-5874-a22b-b4644257ae0f" :question/math-academy-id "e-3339"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f6e70249-58d6-57ce-867c-ff9a3b4219f4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048616}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120354} {:db/id 17592186120498} {:db/id 17592186266148} {:db/id 17592186266149} {:db/id 17592186266150} {:db/id 17592186268851} {:db/id 17592186362218} {:db/id 17592186362219} {:db/id 17592186392898} {:db/id 17592186400653} {:db/id 17592186404933} {:db/id 17592186444693} {:db/id 17592186444694} {:db/id 17592186492055}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Center of the Osculating Circle"} :step/id #uuid "4edcd617-8c81-5a66-b0c0-b9510d42e399" :step/math-academy-id 11121 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120600}} {:db/id 17592186120599 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121010 :tutorial/content "If a curve has a curvature of zero at some point, the radius of curvature at that point is defined to be infinite.

It follows from the definition that a straight line has zero curvature at all of its points. Conversely, if a curve has zero curvature at any point, it must be contained on a straight line.

Suppose now that we want to find the radius of curvature for the curve 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle t^2, \: 1 - t^2, \: 1+ t^2 \right\rangle
$$

at an arbitrary point where $t> 0.$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and its magnitude $\| \mathbf r'(t) \|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,-2t,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the last step, we used the fact that $\sqrt{t^2}=t$ since $t>0.$

Next, we find the unit tangent and its derivative for $t>0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}t}\cdot ⟨2t,\,-2t,\,2t⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨1,-1,1⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(t) & =⟨0,0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}t}{0}=\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, despite its "parabolic" appearance, the given curve is contained on a straight line!

**Note:** Often, the unit tangent vector of a curve $\mathbf T(t)$ may look a bit complicated. In such cases, the following formula involving a cross product may be useful. It says that the radius of curvature of a twice-differentiable curve $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by 

$$
R(t)=  \dfrac{1}{\kappa(t)} =\frac{{{{\left\| {\mathbf r'\left( t \right)} \right\|}^3}}}{{\left\| {\mathbf r'\left( t \right) \times \mathbf r''\left( t \right)} \right\|}}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "590485ba-30a6-549b-a4cf-d6641c92a033" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2490 :tutorial/title "Infinite Radius of Curvature"} :step/id #uuid "5b0a8082-2fe6-5852-b950-a17b2bc3d3ca" :step/math-academy-id 11122} {:db/id 17592186120600 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119760 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119576 :question/id #uuid "8d58f131-7260-5346-9a88-60862c0a1b55" :question/math-academy-id "e-3340"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a053eb10-be16-5423-9b7b-c23677bb6335" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048648}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120381} {:db/id 17592186120558} {:db/id 17592186266137} {:db/id 17592186266138} {:db/id 17592186266139} {:db/id 17592186266140} {:db/id 17592186266141} {:db/id 17592186320790} {:db/id 17592186362307} {:db/id 17592186362308} {:db/id 17592186362317} {:db/id 17592186444695} {:db/id 17592186444697} {:db/id 17592186478445}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Radius of Curvature Using the Cross Product Formula"} :step/id #uuid "25d03bd3-ad37-5232-b295-cdb7c4d45fa8" :step/math-academy-id 11123 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120599}}] :activity/title "Radius of Curvature" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186120034} {:db/id 17592186120595 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121008 :tutorial/content "The **osculating circle** (sometimes called the *kissing circle*) of a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is a circle that

\mathbf r(t) = \bigg\langle t+1, 2- \dfrac{t^2}{2} \bigg\rangle
$$

has the normal vector

$$
\mathbf{N}(t) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+t^2}} \langle -t, \: -1 \rangle ,
$$

and the radius of curvature at the point $P(1,2)$ where $t=0$ is $R(0)=1.$

So, the center of the osculating circle is at the tip of the vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0+1,\,2-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}⟩+1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}}}⟨0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2⟩+⟨0,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the center of the osculating circle at the point where $t=0$ is located at $\left(1, 1 \right),$ as shown below.

"25d03bd3-ad37-5232-b295-cdb7c4d45fa8" :step/math-academy-id 11123 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120599}} {:db/id 17592186120599 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121010 :tutorial/content "If a curve has a curvature of zero at some point, the radius of curvature at that point is defined to be infinite.

It follows from the definition that a straight line has zero curvature at all of its points. Conversely, if a curve has zero curvature at any point, it must be contained on a straight line.

Suppose now that we want to find the radius of curvature for the curve 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle t^2, \: 1 - t^2, \: 1+ t^2 \right\rangle
$$

at an arbitrary point where $t> 0.$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and its magnitude $\| \mathbf r'(t) \|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,-2t,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the last step, we used the fact that $\sqrt{t^2}=t$ since $t>0.$

Next, we find the unit tangent and its derivative for $t>0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}t}\cdot ⟨2t,\,-2t,\,2t⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨1,-1,1⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(t) & =⟨0,0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}t}{0}=\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, despite its "parabolic" appearance, the given curve is contained on a straight line!

**Note:** Often, the unit tangent vector of a curve $\mathbf T(t)$ may look a bit complicated. In such cases, the following formula involving a cross product may be useful. It says that the radius of curvature of a twice-differentiable curve $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by 

$$
R(t)=  \dfrac{1}{\kappa(t)} =\frac{{{{\left\| {\mathbf r'\left( t \right)} \right\|}^3}}}{{\left\| {\mathbf r'\left( t \right) \times \mathbf r''\left( t \right)} \right\|}}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "590485ba-30a6-549b-a4cf-d6641c92a033" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2490 :tutorial/title "Infinite Radius of Curvature"} :step/id #uuid "5b0a8082-2fe6-5852-b950-a17b2bc3d3ca" :step/math-academy-id 11122} {:db/id 17592186121010 :tutorial/content "If a curve has a curvature of zero at some point, the radius of curvature at that point is defined to be infinite.

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "590485ba-30a6-549b-a4cf-d6641c92a033" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2490 :tutorial/title "Infinite Radius of Curvature"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186478469} :activity/id #uuid "721b1290-aefc-5e37-b344-d5131a4a3506" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048339 :topic/id #uuid "96c0d2ef-1891-5083-879c-8dcc09b70542" :topic/math-academy-id 1834} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186478469 :step/content {:db/id 17592186362218 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0589c295-d29a-5525-8df9-84a2fef5c818" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,1)$ and the radius $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$" :db/id 17592186360850} {:answer/id #uuid "07bef1ff-2469-5d35-b897-08a2224bc1bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,1)$ and the radius $\sqrt{2}$" :db/id 17592186360863} {:answer/id #uuid "4e594d6b-dcde-5053-8f5b-521e676bfdea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,0)$ and the radius $\sqrt{2}$" :db/id 17592186361178} {:answer/id #uuid "8d7bf037-7a41-5080-8e72-6de80d6a14df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,-1)$ and the radius $2$" :db/id 17592186361463} {:answer/id #uuid "b5a6e881-f847-56c1-9261-cac4148a3edc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,0)$ and the radius $2$" :db/id 17592186361642}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186360863} :answer-field/id #uuid "8d378b87-11c8-5248-9b4e-02b0168b1e64" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362106}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "24945e7c-95e1-50bc-b79f-c2e7d2556ce8" :question/math-academy-id "q-97593" :question/problem "Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(1,0)$ where $t=0$, given that $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖=\sqrt{2},$ and the unit tangent vector to the curve is

$$
T(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t),$ we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨1,0⟩,$ since the point $P(1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t),$ ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\operatorname{cos}⁡0-\operatorname{sin}⁡0⟩=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1}=\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨1,0⟩+\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,1⟩=⟨0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "02094b1d-f4cb-5c2d-b251-9b08dea3ddda" :step/next {:db/id 17592186478493}} {:db/id 17592186478484 :step/content {:db/id 17592186266149 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "58d19bde-c557-5f9c-8b97-9ee98b0b44b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $⟨0,1⟩$ and the radius is $\sqrt{2}$" :db/id 17592186263763} {:answer/id #uuid "8d133154-399b-5788-8d63-d8c5a7d9ea07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $⟨1,1⟩$ and the radius is $\sqrt{2}$" :db/id 17592186264207} {:answer/id #uuid "975c77d4-38ea-5a25-aa07-13a8a2dc63a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $⟨-1,0⟩$ and the radius is $2$" :db/id 17592186264300} {:answer/id #uuid "b5763ceb-8908-51fe-ab60-358749e774f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $⟨0,-1⟩$ and the radius is $2$" :db/id 17592186264569} {:answer/id #uuid "edaf1b77-f55a-53de-aaf6-870a334b4eb6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $⟨-1,0⟩$ and the radius is $\sqrt{2}$" :db/id 17592186265077}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186265077} :answer-field/id #uuid "61507bf1-0dd4-5fab-a0ea-a38287bd4d32" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265414}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6665004f-e6b2-5e6c-b764-778c8eb359b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-132201" :question/problem "Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,1)$ where $t=0,$ given that $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖=\sqrt{2},$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

$$
T(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨0,1⟩,$ since the point $P(0,1)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,-1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0,1⟩+\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩+⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9eccffe8-ee2f-59ee-9cc6-9c221f7ead6a"} {:db/id 17592186478486 :step/content {:db/id 17592186266140 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18e7b0c5-59c8-5276-8f27-e519196c22e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2}" :db/id 17592186263236} {:answer/id #uuid "5c697a54-9e06-52cc-9c8e-9e93cd4a2158" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}{e}^{\pi }}{2}" :db/id 17592186263796} {:answer/id #uuid "a532f5f7-12c2-5842-a3e6-eb768839607c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2}" :db/id 17592186264413} {:answer/id #uuid "ab6b8756-6f83-5bd9-aa3b-ae5978576099" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{\pi }" :db/id 17592186264473} {:answer/id #uuid "bb8a8631-251a-5a00-aa65-16be619ec141" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}{e}^{-\pi }" :db/id 17592186264630}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264630} :answer-field/id #uuid "805bbad1-9820-5da9-8726-919fd6256468" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265470}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7d2943df-d322-57f9-9465-3be5dfbf7067" :question/math-academy-id "q-132129" :question/problem "Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=\pi $ for the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-t}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-t}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\times 2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$

$$

$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨1,0⟩,$ since the point $P(1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t),$ ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖:$ 

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1}=\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨1,0⟩+\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨-1,1⟩=⟨0,1⟩.\end{aligned}

curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-t}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-t}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & ={e}^{-\pi }⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\times 2{e}^{-\pi }⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\,\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =2{e}^{-2\pi }k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2{e}^{-2\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖} \\  & =\frac{({e}^{-\pi }\sqrt{2})^{3}}{2{e}^{-2\pi }} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}{e}^{-3\pi }}{2{e}^{-2\pi }} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{-\pi }.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{3}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t-3{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}){sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-3{cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}){cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-3{sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨6(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}){(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}-3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{3},6(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}){(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}-3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ and ${r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩\times (\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & ={(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4})}^{2}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \,-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}\,-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{8}\cdot 2\,k \\  & =-\frac{9}{4}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})\times {r}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}=\frac{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{3}}{\,\frac{9}{4}\,}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "360756d1-180d-59b9-adc1-f4b18b0a5d95"} {:db/id 17592186492091 :step/content {:db/id 17592186492052 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06c981d0-879c-5395-961f-18d30c7ee1c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186491467} {:answer/id #uuid "30ccc38c-3c4b-51d7-a8be-015493817d8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186491550} {:answer/id #uuid "ca9407b6-9b59-518b-866e-5aec8e95de1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{\sqrt{33}}" :db/id 17592186491798} {:answer/id #uuid "cbceddc2-2b0f-51bf-9732-a4901abca037" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2\sqrt{6}}" :db/id 17592186491799} {:answer/id #uuid "f4c914c6-693e-5352-8b50-6792d0a0a2ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2\sqrt{6}}" :db/id 17592186491872}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186491467} :answer-field/id #uuid "49d0d86a-f951-5330-9b83-6ded6a5ca5d3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186491911}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c0a58b0a-c208-5232-9cb9-1df706de5400" :question/math-academy-id "q-34618" :question/problem "Find the radius of curvature for the curve $r(t)$ at the point $r(0)$ if the curve and the derivative ${T}^{′}(t)$ of the corresponding unit tangent vector are given by

$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the curve $r(t)$ and the derivative ${T}^{′}(t)$ of the unit tangent, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{2t},\,1⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨2{e}^{0},\,2{e}^{0},\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate ${T}^{′}(0)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(0) & =\frac{2}{(2{e}^{0}+1)^{2}}⟨{e}^{0}-2{e}^{0},\,2{e}^{0},\,-2{e}^{0}⟩ \\  & =\frac{2}{9}⟨-1,\,2,\,-2⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{2}{9}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\frac{2}{9}\sqrt{9}=\frac{2\cdot 3}{9}=\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the curve $r(t)$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of the osculating circle: 

$$

$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡2t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "9c6ec06b-19b9-5029-9158-da22d4a86ae0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186492109}} {:db/id 17592186492107 :step/content {:db/id 17592186362219 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ff6569a-4cab-5e8f-8762-376041784c00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(\pi ,-2)$ and the radius $4$" :db/id 17592186360893} {:answer/id #uuid "35e1a2f8-2f8a-5d39-9327-ca2e3e8e0ee6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(\pi ,0)$ and the radius $\frac{1}{4}$" :db/id 17592186361077} {:answer/id #uuid "7ed54666-3b56-576a-9615-df8106a5c984" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(\pi ,0)$ and the radius $4$" :db/id 17592186361398} {:answer/id #uuid "7fa0a898-43f7-561b-bd46-61b1497e96c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(\pi ,-1)$ and the radius $2$" :db/id 17592186361406} {:answer/id #uuid "f9ad7825-cc9e-5adb-aafe-2969fcf48b7b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(\pi ,1)$ and the radius $2$" :db/id 17592186361955}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186360893} :answer-field/id #uuid "b90568e4-8415-56af-8bbd-a969ac099004" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362151}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4602817c-a855-5ccd-8d1a-bca1a25a4651" :question/math-academy-id "q-97594" :question/problem "Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(\pi ,2)$ where $t=\pi $, given that $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖=2,$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

$$
T(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2})⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(\pi )=⟨\pi ,2⟩$,  since the point $P(\pi ,2)$ is at the tip of $r(\pi ).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t),$ ${T}^{′}(\pi )$ and $‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2}),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩=\frac{1}{2}⟨0,-1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖}{‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖}=\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{2})}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=\pi $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\pi ) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\pi )}{‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖}=\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})}⟨0,-1⟩=⟨0,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "d21bdd95-0820-5dce-89ad-01f22a360825" :step/next {:db/id 17592186492088}} {:db/id 17592186492109 :step/content {:db/id 17592186492055 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1060224c-d0b3-5776-a766-96b15404205d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(2,0)$ and the radius is $2$" :db/id 17592186491485} {:answer/id #uuid "28349558-5db2-5c09-8b29-f853f31f0913" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(2,0)$ and the radius is $4$" :db/id 17592186491537} {:answer/id #uuid "31280857-9970-5bf7-888c-fc39c357541b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(2,2)$ and the radius is $\sqrt{2}$" :db/id 17592186491551} {:answer/id #uuid "5611b291-95d5-535d-999e-5155c671c2b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(-2,0)$ and the radius is $2$" :db/id 17592186491619} {:answer/id #uuid "910409ee-6695-5f67-a309-77a3fe4d5eb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,2)$ and the radius is $2$" :db/id 17592186491701}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186491485} :answer-field/id #uuid "7fa7d73e-6b11-5043-84cc-72ac6b11b133" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186491930}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cb82f4d9-80ff-57cb-8e48-0da61beda250" :question/math-academy-id "q-97585" :question/problem "Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(2,2)$ where $t=2$, given that $‖{r}^{′}(2)‖=1,$ and the unit tangent vector to the curve is

$$

Notice that $r(2)=⟨2,2⟩,$ since the point $P(2,2)$ is at the tip of $r(2).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t),$ ${T}^{′}(2)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(2)‖:$

$$

$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(2) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(2)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(2)‖}=\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=2.\end{aligned}

$$

"Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(2,2)$ where $t=2$, given that $‖{r}^{′}(2)‖=1,$ and the unit tangent vector to the curve is

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(2)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(2)=⟨2,2⟩,$ since the point $P(2,2)$ is at the tip of $r(2).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t),$ ${T}^{′}(2)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(2)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{4t-{t}^{2}}}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2-t}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2-t}{2\sqrt{4t-{t}^{2}}},\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(2) & =⟨\frac{2-2}{2\sqrt{4(2)-{2}^{2}}},\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩=⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(2)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(2) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(2)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(2)‖}=\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=2$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(2) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(2)}{‖{T}^{′}(2)‖}=\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩=⟨0,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2)+R(2)N(2) & =⟨2,2⟩+2⟨0,-1⟩=⟨2,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e0ee45a0-d850-5a33-afdc-ce8ffcb1cb89" :step/next {:db/id 17592186492107}} {:db/id 17592186492107 :step/content {:db/id 17592186362219 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ff6569a-4cab-5e8f-8762-376041784c00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(\pi ,-2)$ and the radius $4$" :db/id 17592186360893} {:answer/id #uuid "35e1a2f8-2f8a-5d39-9327-ca2e3e8e0ee6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(\pi ,0)$ and the radius $\frac{1}{4}$" :db/id 17592186361077} {:answer/id #uuid "7ed54666-3b56-576a-9615-df8106a5c984" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(\pi ,0)$ and the radius $4$" :db/id 17592186361398} {:answer/id #uuid "7fa0a898-43f7-561b-bd46-61b1497e96c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(\pi ,-1)$ and the radius $2$" :db/id 17592186361406} {:answer/id #uuid "f9ad7825-cc9e-5adb-aafe-2969fcf48b7b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(\pi ,1)$ and the radius $2$" :db/id 17592186361955}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186360893} :answer-field/id #uuid "b90568e4-8415-56af-8bbd-a969ac099004" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362151}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4602817c-a855-5ccd-8d1a-bca1a25a4651" :question/math-academy-id "q-97594" :question/problem "Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(\pi ,2)$ where $t=\pi $, given that $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖=2,$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2}),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩=\frac{1}{2}⟨0,-1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖}{‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖}=\frac{2}{(\frac{1}{2})}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=\pi $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\pi ) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\pi )}{‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖}=\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})}⟨0,-1⟩=⟨0,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi )+R(\pi )N(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,2⟩+4⟨0,-1⟩=⟨\pi ,-2⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
C=\{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\}.
$$

Find the matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the map $T:V\to {R}^{2}$ relative to these bases if 

$$
T({b}_{1})=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,T({b}_{2})=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $[T]_{B|C}$ is the matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $C.$

First, we need to find the coordinates of $T({b}_{i})$ relative to the basis $C$ for each $i=1,2.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the following matrix:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) \\ | & | & | & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 9 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the right-hand side gives the matrix of the linear transformation relative to the bases $B$ and $C:$

$$
[T]_{B|C}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0b3a2889-b1be-57f0-91ef-41940e81fc0b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186501265}} {:db/id 17592186501257 :step/content {:db/id 17592186362216 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4176c859-5854-5080-bf2e-b0f94f0b8361" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186361127} {:answer/id #uuid "6cb06e3c-e23d-5e91-bbec-4e481c417779" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186361321} {:answer/id #uuid "7eaadcc6-81a8-5407-bdd2-2c06f604c335" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -8 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186361396} {:answer/id #uuid "a69c20d3-4c5a-587d-8103-f2c720627c8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186361584} {:answer/id #uuid "d8ce3e71-5c81-5e9f-a3e1-5fabb47b6eec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -11 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186361801}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361801} :answer-field/id #uuid "2eea433c-814e-5e0e-919d-f13b06399a26" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362027}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c64bcdb5-768e-5293-a151-ad4d8fbb8250" :question/math-academy-id "q-97579" :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ (shown above) and a basis $C$ of ${R}^{3}.$
The matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the linear map $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{3}$ relative to these bases, and the vector $x\in {R}^{2},$ are also given. Find $[T(x)]_{C}.$" :question/worked-solution "We can find the coordinates of the image of $x$ under $T$ relative to the basis $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B}\end{aligned}

First, we need to find $[x]_{B},$ the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B.$ So, let

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1} &=-4 \\ -2{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=-3.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & -4 \\ -2 & 5 & -3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 4 \\ -2 & 5 & -3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 & 5\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 5 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
C=\{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\}.
$$

Find the matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the map $T:V\to {R}^{2}$ relative to these bases if 

$$
T({b}_{1})=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,T({b}_{2})=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
