$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) \\ | & | & | & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 9 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the right-hand side gives the matrix of the linear transformation relative to the bases $B$ and $C:$

$$
[T]_{B|C}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0b3a2889-b1be-57f0-91ef-41940e81fc0b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186501265}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3811dc15-f044-5933-86e0-b81332887411" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}, & 0<x<1 \\ \frac{1}{2x}, & 1\le x<e\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

 

We compute the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{e}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{e}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{e}x\cdot \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}+{\frac{x}{2}|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{e}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{2e-1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4a878e04-e7e6-5c4d-a22c-de06d29307c3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436288}} {:db/id 17592186436286 :step/content {:db/id 17592186436282 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12065d32-e113-5992-bb8d-f535e75fb9ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{2}" :db/id 17592186436257} {:answer/id #uuid "18efb766-1d3d-58da-bff5-d24f02292777" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186436258} {:answer/id #uuid "29173ece-c32d-5596-a3a8-34d0349c05ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/id 17592186436259} {:answer/id #uuid "a2a8b51a-6b08-55ab-89b7-ef577ff59874" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{8}" :db/id 17592186436268} {:answer/id #uuid "b73c6eb0-be0e-57a4-8c3b-4e4f51c6378c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186436269}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186436257} :answer-field/id #uuid "76d69cbc-7ea6-5219-b9fe-b27e60e2aa63" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186436277}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c64c8376-4f9a-5df0-81b9-bf811d12f7ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-152904" :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[4X+2].$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}, & 0<x\le 1, \\ \frac{1}{2{x}^{3}}, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of the expected value:

$$
\text{E}[4X+2]=4\text{E}[X]+2
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{3}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }x\cdot \frac{1}{2{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3x}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{3{x}^{2}}{8})|}_{0}^{1}+{(-\frac{1}{2x})|}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =(\frac{3}{8}-0)+(0-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4X+2] & =4\text{E}[X]+2 \\  & =4\cdot \frac{7}{8}+2 \\  & =\frac{11}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5cb7073d-7ea9-5c29-94c4-88d377c15dab" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436287}} {:db/id 17592186436287 :step/content {:db/id 17592186436283 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "30945d0b-c228-50cd-9399-4fc6759027b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186436260} {:answer/id #uuid "477a366f-5027-5734-8066-1c5b19a5ae4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{8}" :db/id 17592186436262} {:answer/id #uuid "52eacba8-2ac3-5a25-85fe-9c675a072c68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186436263} {:answer/id #uuid "5ffc82d5-d3b0-5643-95db-cbc049b36c70" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{9}" :db/id 17592186436264} {:answer/id #uuid "c10ec2db-f24e-557d-8a16-961d2cfcd677" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186436270}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186436260} :answer-field/id #uuid "a9112695-ad08-5300-a06c-ea0b770acb45" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186436278}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "edac9b93-8284-5302-bc8b-9583d4ecc8f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-152907" :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[12X-8].$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}, & 0<x\le 1, \\ \frac{8}{9}, & 1\le x<2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of the expected value:

$$
\text{E}[12X-8]=12\text{E}[X]-8
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{8}{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{8x}{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{4}}{12})|}_{0}^{1}+{\frac{4{x}^{2}}{9}|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{12}-0)+(\frac{16}{9}-\frac{4}{9}) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}+\frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{17}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}x\cdot \frac{e}{e{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{e}{ex-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{e}{e-1}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{e}{e-1}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{e}{e-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2e-(e-1)X] & =2e-(e-1)\text{E}[X] \\  & =2e-(e-1)\cdot \frac{e}{e-1} \\  & =2e-e \\  & =e.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d8cd80ec-e90e-5ae1-afb0-eecf1d561a37" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436286}}] :activity/title "Expected Values of Continuous Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186436255} {:db/id 17592186436284 :step/content {:db/id 17592186436280 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01b4f1c9-6a5b-52c7-aa2b-f725b7d61594" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2.87" :db/id 17592186436256} {:answer/id #uuid "3cd6386a-9b90-5c4e-be0a-bdee4537678d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.54" :db/id 17592186436261} {:answer/id #uuid "6b109b1d-9413-505f-ad96-a041eb6ca00e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.02" :db/id 17592186436265} {:answer/id #uuid "e329b197-e48b-55a0-8164-4bc46b1e5644" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1.12" :db/id 17592186436273} {:answer/id #uuid "e4dba7f7-2146-5ff3-a626-ce33b04b8a0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2.30" :db/id 17592186436274}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186436265} :answer-field/id #uuid "aded4a40-1d18-5fec-bc4b-4bcb36ab2d42" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186436279}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "26e02fce-e08e-5fe6-a3ec-6ad998577401" :question/math-academy-id "q-90448" :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[X].$ Give your answer rounded to two decimal places.

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{3}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }x\cdot \frac{1}{2{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3x}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{3{x}^{2}}{8})|}_{0}^{1}+{(-\frac{1}{2x})|}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =(\frac{3}{8}-0)+(0-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4X+2] & =4\text{E}[X]+2 \\  & =4\cdot \frac{7}{8}+2 \\  & =\frac{11}{2}.\end{aligned}

"edac9b93-8284-5302-bc8b-9583d4ecc8f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-152907" :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[12X-8].$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}, & 0<x\le 1, \\ \frac{8}{9}, & 1\le x<2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we simplify using the properties of the expected value:

$$
\text{E}[12X-8]=12\text{E}[X]-8
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{8}{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{8x}{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{4}}{12})|}_{0}^{1}+{\frac{4{x}^{2}}{9}|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{12}-0)+(\frac{16}{9}-\frac{4}{9}) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}+\frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{17}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[12X-8] & =12\text{E}[X]-8 \\  & =12\cdot \frac{17}{12}-8 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "95f58f9a-4473-5f86-8f32-f1873a14a714"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "30945d0b-c228-50cd-9399-4fc6759027b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :step/content {:db/id 17592186121027 :tutorial/content "**Cramer's Rule** is a method for solving a linear system of equations using determinants.

Suppose we have a square system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y &={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y &={b}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where ![](images/c7/c7ef883a1d4dd8c1fc0fc8fbde5ed80c9a5229650fc77c77559b71552370c35b.svg) Then Cramer's rule states that

$$
x =  \dfrac{D_x}{D}, \qquad y = \dfrac{D_y}{D}
$$

is the unique solution of the system, where
![](images/b1/b13ecd10395fe0977d04d627179667cbca207fcf4015a89d43df0e69765f1f5e.svg)

For example, let's use Cramer's rule to solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x-2y &=-1 \\ -1x+2y &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start by finding the **determinant of the coefficient matrix**:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $D_x$ and $D_y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x} & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 2-3\cdot (-2) \\  & =4 \\ {D}_{y} & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to the system is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{D}_{x}}{D}=\frac{4}{4}=1, \\ y & =\frac{{D}_{y}}{D}=\frac{8}{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

It is common to write the solutions to a linear system as a vector. So, in this case, we have

$$
\left< x,y \right> = \left< 1,2 \right>.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3adc5c1c-58e5-5c0a-a8f7-da6abd6f06e2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3102 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "48887938-d6a0-5822-b084-3bf10a3a4461" :step/math-academy-id 16830 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120731}} {:db/id 17592186120731 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119844 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119658 :question/id #uuid "d81e32a1-bd93-5a95-bb4a-e8df9063b5aa" :question/math-academy-id "e-5230"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e7580024-f357-57d4-94f2-85c25e2c144b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049044}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120446} {:db/id 17592186120447} {:db/id 17592186271976} {:db/id 17592186329671} {:db/id 17592186329672} {:db/id 17592186338763} {:db/id 17592186338764} {:db/id 17592186392541} {:db/id 17592186402854}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Parts of Cramer's Rule Formula"} :step/id #uuid "720a6f93-380c-5e70-8c81-e99f44a4ef11" :step/math-academy-id 19262 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120647}}] :activity/title "Cramer's Rule for 2x2 Systems of Linear Equations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186119997} {:db/id 17592186120652 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121027 :tutorial/content "**Cramer's Rule** is a method for solving a linear system of equations using determinants.

$$
y(x) = Ae^{cx} + Bxe^{cx}.
$$

To illustrate, let's solve the following ODE:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 9y =0.
$$

Assuming a solution of the form $y=e^{\lambda x},$ we differentiate and substitute into the ODE:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-6\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+9{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $e^{\lambda x}$ is never zero, we can divide by it to get the **characteristic equation**:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

so $\lambda = 3$ is a **repeated root**. Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x) = Ae^{3x} + Bxe^{3x}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a4fc9c29-f54a-5346-b7b3-59abdf8bb39f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4049 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0a076b74-a850-5e47-b647-e51c36c1259a" :step/math-academy-id $\lambda = c,$ the general solution is

$$
y(x) = Ae^{cx} + Bxe^{cx}.
$$

To illustrate, let's solve the following ODE:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 9y =0.
$$

Assuming a solution of the form $y=e^{\lambda x},$ we differentiate and substitute into the ODE:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-6\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+9{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $e^{\lambda x}$ is never zero, we can divide by it to get the **characteristic equation**:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

so $\lambda = 3$ is a **repeated root**. Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x) = Ae^{3x} + Bxe^{3x}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a4fc9c29-f54a-5346-b7b3-59abdf8bb39f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4049 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0a076b74-a850-5e47-b647-e51c36c1259a" :step/math-academy-id 24226 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088644}} {:db/id 17592186088941 :tutorial/content "When the characteristic equation of a second-order homogeneous ODE has a **repeated root** $\lambda = c,$ the general solution is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-5\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+\frac{25}{4}{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +\frac{25}{4}) & =0.\end{aligned}

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +\frac{25}{4}=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -\frac{5}{2})(\lambda -\frac{5}{2}) & =0 \\ {(\lambda -\frac{5}{2})}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\lambda =\frac{5}{2}$ is a repeated root.

$$

If we are told that one of the eigenvalues of this matrix is $\lambda = 3,$ how do we calculate the corresponding eigenvector?

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 6 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 3 & -4\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 & -8 \\ 0 & -3 & 6 \\ 0 & 3 & -7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find the eigenvectors, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -3{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}-7{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -7 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In this reduced matrix, there are two pivot columns (the $2$nd and $3$rd). Thus, $x_1$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have $x_3 = 0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain $x_2 = 0.$ Therefore, the general solution is

![](images/70/705dd92c7330897f35671b66866791160b9d7f65e3280d5ccb9d992405c08942.svg)

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda  & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(2)(2)) & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 0 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{5}{3} & -\frac{20}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=4{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}(-2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2(4{x}_{3})-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =-4{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-4{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$

:db/id 17592186381112}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c980d806-f256-5388-b798-65b34624c78e" :question/math-academy-id "q-140722" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}3-\lambda  & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )[(3-\lambda )^{2}-1] & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}-(2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$"} :step/id #uuid "54a37441-fb97-5482-8800-e7be9eb1f718"} {:db/id 17592186539070 :step/content {:db/id 17592186392038 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "13304c66-59ed-5804-b519-223c3709ae32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186392040} {:answer/id #uuid "317f7bc8-17c3-5b65-8500-5bfb85e37bde" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186392041} {:answer/id #uuid "808dfd35-c7cf-5560-bba9-dfef1206fd03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186392042} {:answer/id #uuid "94090702-def0-5eac-8760-9a3b321889de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186392043} {:answer/id #uuid "7cb0fced-9501-56c9-8088-68d6df8fb853" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186392044}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186392042} :answer-field/id #uuid "60b86f5a-a5c7-5a8b-9d41-513f5f26be40" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186392039}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ad9f3c50-0a7e-56b3-becb-281cac541291" :question/math-academy-id "q-36973" :question/problem "$$

What is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "Since $A$ is a lower triangular matrix, we have that its eigenvalues are the entries in the main diagonal, that is, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

Also, since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =6.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -5 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{1} &=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}-11{x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+5{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{c}=\frac{0}{1}=0.$"} :step/id #uuid "79acdebf-dccc-5a6c-84a3-c4482c1dbcac" :step/next {:db/id 17592186539082}} {:db/id 17592186539082 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323913 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26853257-a15d-56bd-baf3-05cb4af2b356" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186321448} {:answer/id #uuid "6215dc3a-949b-5a88-b400-1754de3451a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186321914} {:answer/id #uuid "8f37a9ee-9183-5f94-b9e6-589f18d0723c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186322284} {:answer/id #uuid "97007dd8-0a0c-5e5d-b2fe-2c703399817a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186322352} {:answer/id #uuid "e831241f-8157-56bb-8b58-0b3139bec9f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186322966}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186321448} :answer-field/id #uuid "001c22af-200a-5e74-a872-4fc6a4c58849" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323165}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "b75fe299-3a00-56ce-ac2b-3a6b8472e075" :question/math-academy-id "q-37401" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & 3 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((-1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-(3)(2)) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -10) & =0 \\ -(\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -4{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{12}{5}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$

$$

$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{2}:=(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.

What is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "Since $A$ is a lower triangular matrix, we have that its eigenvalues are the entries in the main diagonal, that is, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

Also, since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =6.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -5 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{1} &=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}-11{x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+5{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{c}=\frac{0}{1}=0.$"} :step/id #uuid "79acdebf-dccc-5a6c-84a3-c4482c1dbcac" :step/next {:db/id 17592186539082}} {:db/id 17592186539060 :step/content {:db/id 17592186381111 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2118b9d8-3a94-5241-ac9a-03c1a8165254" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186381113} {:answer/id #uuid "7efa2077-efeb-556a-bdf6-a527627aa068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186381114} {:answer/id #uuid "ebe1eecd-6744-563e-a0ca-489b943e4e23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186381115} {:answer/id #uuid "1b5cac8f-2fc0-5759-807f-d9ee28d2044f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186381116} {:answer/id #uuid "c81fa2d6-7df9-5381-b5a7-f75a91e5988d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186381117}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186381113} :answer-field/id #uuid "b84bb508-82f8-5a30-b1a6-92bf25dfe082" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186381112}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c980d806-f256-5388-b798-65b34624c78e" :question/math-academy-id "q-140722" :question/problem "$$

What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}3-\lambda  & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )[(3-\lambda )^{2}-1] & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}-(2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$"} :step/id #uuid "54a37441-fb97-5482-8800-e7be9eb1f718"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2118b9d8-3a94-5241-ac9a-03c1a8165254" :answer/type {:db/id "q-37401" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda  & 3 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((-1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-(3)(2)) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -10) & =0 \\ -(\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -4{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{12}{5}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "9de96552-9aff-59f8-bf73-97a5a9a29e02" :step/next {:db/id 17592186539107}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid What is the $9$th term?" :question/worked-solution "The first term is $a_1=2$, and the common ratio is $r=3$, so we can write the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot r^{n - 1} \\
&= 2 \cdot 3^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

To find the $9$th term, we can use this formula with

$$
n={\color{blue}9}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= 2 \cdot 3^{n - 1} \\
a_{9} &= 2 \cdot 3^{9 - 1} \\
&= 2 \cdot 3^{8} \\
&= 2 \cdot 6561 \\
&= 13122
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $9$th term is

$$
a_{9}=13\,122
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050977} {:db/id 17592186078796 :question/id #uuid "a3e4bab7-db95-5b0c-996e-e7de8b2baebe" :question/math-academy-id "q-231754"} {:db/id 17592186078891 :question/id #uuid "9aa8020e-093c-5eb5-a959-7b89f61b0d24" :question/math-academy-id "q-39439"} {:db/id 17592186078893 :question/id #uuid "9147c54e-ff48-5b40-9282-e0e71d048a38" :question/math-academy-id "q-39440"} {:db/id 17592186078559 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078204 :question/id #uuid "4bf89b8f-f713-51b5-8536-5aa5b08f16d3" :question/math-academy-id "e-1511"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5760a53a-1a0c-568e-ac9c-c820eaad3010" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050668}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078797 :question/id #uuid "15178543-fce2-524a-bf78-a8e6e6bf0c75" :question/math-academy-id "q-231755"} {:db/id 17592186078798 :question/id #uuid "21558128-4b83-5d8f-bfc1-d211399f1149" :question/math-academy-id "q-231756"} {:db/id 17592186079226 :question/id #uuid "8554fab9-1eda-57c4-8807-00ec9a2fdd05" :question/math-academy-id "q-9469"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Formula for the Nth Term of a Geometric Sequence"} {:db/id 17592186078204 :question/id #uuid "4bf89b8f-f713-51b5-8536-5aa5b08f16d3" :question/math-academy-id "e-1511" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186078559 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5760a53a-1a0c-568e-ac9c-c820eaad3010" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Formula for the Nth Term of a Geometric Sequence"}] :question/problem "Find the formula for the $n$th term of a sequence if the $6$th term is $80$ and the common ratio is $-2$." :question/worked-solution "The common ratio is $r=-2$, so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot r^{n - 1} \\
&= a_{1} \cdot (-2)^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

However, we still need to figure out the first term $a_1$. We know that the $6$th term is $a_6=80$, so we can solve for the first term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{6} &= a_{1} \cdot (-2)^{6 - 1} \\
80 &= a_{1} \cdot (-2)^{5} \\
80 &= a_{1} \cdot (-32) \\
- \frac{80}{32} &= a_{1} \\
- \frac{5}{2} &= a_{1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the first term is

$$
a_1=-\dfrac{5}{2}
$$

we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot (-2)^{n - 1} \\
&=-\frac{5}{2} \cdot (-2)^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify a bit further by manipulating the exponents, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= -\frac{5}{2}(-2)^{n - 1} \\
&= 5 \cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \cdot (-2)^{n - 1} \\
&= 5 \cdot (-2)^{-1} \cdot (-2)^{n - 1} \\
&= 5 \cdot (-2)^{n - 2}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186078797 :question/id #uuid "15178543-fce2-524a-bf78-a8e6e6bf0c75" :question/math-academy-id "q-231755"} {:db/id 17592186078798 :question/id #uuid "21558128-4b83-5d8f-bfc1-d211399f1149" :question/math-academy-id "q-231756"} {:db/id 17592186079226 :question/id #uuid "8554fab9-1eda-57c4-8807-00ec9a2fdd05" :question/math-academy-id "q-9469"} {:db/id 17592186078560 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078203 :question/id #uuid "f7b26998-6137-54f9-bfe1-a2c3ba5eb0f9" :question/math-academy-id "e-1510"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d82eb202-fec9-5769-a006-67d42b932303" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078799 :question/id #uuid "6635ce75-68d9-56d3-9e68-8210fcf2e22a" :question/math-academy-id "q-231757"} {:db/id 17592186078800 :question/id #uuid "7a3af20c-e402-5825-898f-5f46de496b91" :question/math-academy-id "q-231759"} {:db/id 17592186079094 :question/id #uuid "ca6cdfec-1f4f-5cdc-a93c-d4d4bc37addd" :question/math-academy-id "q-5357"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Particular Term of a Geometric Sequence Given a Term and the Common Ratio"} {:db/id 17592186078203 :question/id #uuid "f7b26998-6137-54f9-bfe1-a2c3ba5eb0f9" :question/math-academy-id "e-1510" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186078560 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d82eb202-fec9-5769-a006-67d42b932303" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Particular Term of a Geometric Sequence Given a Term and the Common Ratio"}] :question/problem "Given that the $5$th term of a geometric sequence is $9$, and the common ratio is $3$, find the second term." :question/worked-solution "The common ratio is $r=3$, so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot r^{n - 1} \\
&= a_{1} \cdot 3^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

However, we still need to figure out the first term $a_1$. We know that the $5$th term is $a_5=9$, so we can solve for the first term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{5} &= a_{1} \cdot 3^{5 - 1} \\
9 &= a_{1} \cdot 3^{4} \\
9 &= a_{1} \cdot 81 \\
\frac{9}{81} &= a_{1} \\
\frac{1}{9} &= a_{1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the first term is

$$
a_1=\dfrac{1}{9}
$$

we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot 3^{n - 1} \\
&= \frac{1}{9} \cdot 3^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can use this formula to compute the second term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{2} &= \frac{1}{9} \cdot 3^{2 - 1} \\
&= \frac{1}{9} \cdot 3 \\
&= \frac{1}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second term is

$$
a_2 = \dfrac{1}{3}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186078799 :question/id #uuid "6635ce75-68d9-56d3-9e68-8210fcf2e22a" :question/math-academy-id "q-231757"} {:db/id 17592186078800 :question/id #uuid "7a3af20c-e402-5825-898f-5f46de496b91" :question/math-academy-id "q-231759"} {:db/id 17592186079094 :question/id #uuid "ca6cdfec-1f4f-5cdc-a93c-d4d4bc37addd" :question/math-academy-id "q-5357"} {:db/id 17592186048142} {:db/id 17592186049076} {:db/id 17592186050155} {:db/id 17592186050598} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186079501} :activity/id #uuid "9b5429f3-219e-5e7d-8ead-04a47137510b" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050067 :topic/id #uuid "2a8497f4-0ed3-5e71-a11d-456426f348f7" :topic/math-academy-id 680} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186079501 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079626 :tutorial/content "The general formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is

$$
a_n = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

To illustrate how this works, suppose we want to find the $10$th term of the following geometric sequence:

$$
3, \: 6, \: 12, \: \ldots
$$

The first term is $a_1=3$, and the common ratio is $r=2$, so we can write the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot r^{n - 1} \\
&= 3 \cdot 2^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
n={\color{blue}10}

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= 3 \cdot 2^{n - 1} \\
a_{10} &= 3 \cdot 2^{10 - 1} \\
&= 3 \cdot 2^{9} \\
&= 3 \cdot 512 \\
&= 1536
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $10$th term is

$$
a_{10}=1\,536
$$

![](images/61/6130842f788070c7e97fe82698b701293af681a6aba3acfce0f4dde269cddbcf.png)

$$
y = -a(b^x) + k.
$$

This is the equation of a reflected exponential graph $y=-a(b^x)$ that is translated $k$ units up." :tutorial/id #uuid "73a5f011-6c32-5204-b086-8c7c7a7bdead" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14028 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/73/73c6a8268a179f72611fb65e099d1249d48501e4fd4731d03747800e1944fd97.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(1,2)$ to the point $D(1,3).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{7}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(2x-3y)\,i+(x+y)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$  It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨0,1⟩+t(⟨1,2⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\  & =⟨t,1+t⟩ \\  & =t\,i+(1+t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=t$ and $y=1+t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =(2x-3y)\,i+(x+y)\,j \\  & =(2t-3(1+t))\,i+(t+(1+t))\,j \\  & =(-3-t)\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =((-3-t)\,i+(2t+1)\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =-3-t+2t+1 \\  & =t-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{7}{2} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-2)\,\text{d}t+\frac{7}{2} \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-2t]}_{0}^{1}+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-2-0]+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{7}{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345283 :question/id #uuid "616650f8-c315-5a80-80b8-1d1e65ec51b4" :question/math-academy-id "q-77180" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179669 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5ce5418-6b75-5efa-b7f9-99ee16c510be" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3f99a0c2-ff39-555f-979d-c5dceb67d68c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186342761} {:answer/id #uuid "561cf640-b717-5a0c-a5a7-05b94a807500" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186342954} {:answer/id #uuid "b645e1eb-5ce9-56ca-8d1b-c4fb928eafdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186343836} {:answer/id #uuid "d687ba62-fd77-5fb2-85a6-257e3f469e25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186344120} {:answer/id #uuid "ece5dfda-1ddb-554b-acda-daf0da60f92e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186344318}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "3f99a0c2-ff39-555f-979d-c5dceb67d68c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186342761} :answer-field/id #uuid "9ab12311-2d02-5230-960f-45a14af856ac" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186344760}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/93/93c6184f39b28a057866bb02e11e5e81a7abea4ff8a9a907670dd30cfc93d557.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(1,-1)$ to the point $B(1,1),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(1,1)$ to the point $O(0,0).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(2x+y)\,i+(x-2y)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment from $B$ to $O.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(0-b) \\  & =⟨1,1⟩+t(⟨0,0⟩-⟨1,1⟩) \\  & =⟨1-t,1-t⟩ \\  & =(1-t)\,i+(1-t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=1-t$ and $y=1-t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(2x+y)\,i+(x-2y)\,j \\  & =(2(1-t)+(1-t))\,i+((1-t)-2(1-t))\,j \\  & =(3-3t)\,i+(-1+t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =((3-3t)\,i+(-1+t)\,j)\cdot (-i-j) \\  & =-3+3t+1-t \\  & =-2+2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2+2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+(-2t+{t}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2+(1-2) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345284 :question/id #uuid "b2144499-6ba0-5eff-ada5-d16752f7b523" :question/math-academy-id "q-77182" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179669 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5ce5418-6b75-5efa-b7f9-99ee16c510be" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21279c87-66bb-50e4-8d0a-b4f4a20df582" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{8}{3}" :db/id 17592186342511} {:answer/id #uuid "56b72719-148e-5b84-8585-452f45bb273d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{8}{5}" :db/id 17592186342960} {:answer/id #uuid "5c203805-aaee-5456-a95d-7a12caeeb4c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186343009} {:answer/id #uuid "683b017e-1f61-5d0d-8485-fec00b137cb3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186343128} {:answer/id #uuid "fb4af7cc-9165-5222-ac1c-d3e9cde8c428" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186344449}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "21279c87-66bb-50e4-8d0a-b4f4a20df582" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{8}{3}" :db/id 17592186342511} :answer-field/id #uuid "22e376b5-f6bc-5044-8715-29e828c6d70a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186344556}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/60/6087da076e65bda5240c428ff67c570ad59ae9a8e5a5a3c9e8406184998de56a.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(1,0),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(1,0)$ to the point $B(0,-2).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{7}{3},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=({x}^{2}+y)\,i+(x-{y}^{2})\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the horizontal line segment from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t) & =0+t(a-0) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,0⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨t,0⟩ \\  & =t\,i,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=t$ and $y=0.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =({x}^{2}+y)\,i+(x-{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =({t}^{2}+0)\,i+(t-{0}^{2})\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)j \\  & =i\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =({t}^{2}\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i) \\  & ={t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{7}{3} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-0)+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345285 :question/id #uuid "60807a56-8605-5f52-976b-4c6cebda8f0a" :question/math-academy-id "q-77185"} {:db/id 17592186345286 :question/id #uuid "8fc56ee5-fc5d-5429-bfdb-4254f7ee30fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-77191"} {:db/id 17592186415770 :question/id #uuid "3412530f-81b3-51bb-95a9-4599a55eb207" :question/math-academy-id "q-77250"} {:db/id 17592186415774 :question/id #uuid "8399ab15-70cf-5db8-b1d1-61088de736be" :question/math-academy-id "q-77244"} {:db/id 17592186424621 :question/id #uuid "515517e3-98f2-5a9f-ba03-8d3b47263ffd" :question/math-academy-id "q-77258" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23b97760-1703-5852-afc4-69acd21e7cc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186424603} {:answer/id #uuid "4bd6afbc-8569-51f5-a569-dd388d648b11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186424605} {:answer/id #uuid "79d50006-6f06-56c3-bce2-b65f3e1eb21c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186424607} {:answer/id #uuid "d37fe04f-4a91-5f51-9524-f7477c2a7f9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186424612} {:answer/id #uuid "e17522ae-4622-53a9-bb60-7bec4bbcce91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186424613}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424605} :answer-field/id #uuid "7fdba31b-0f4f-583e-a52e-f0510ad8e3c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424617}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "![](images/4d/4d4c2c86ed8506ff034141ac20a5a56587a80370384ceeaf08c66f2ce3e8a315.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a section of the parabola $y=-\sqrt{x}$ from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(4,-2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(4,-2)$ to the point $B(4,0).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{8}{3},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the section of the curve $y=-\sqrt{x}$ from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t)=t\,i-\sqrt{t}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 4.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=-\sqrt{t}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =t\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{t})j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,j) \\  & =t-\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{8}{3} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t-\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2})\text{d}t+\frac{8}{3} \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{t}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{0}^{4}+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{4}^{3/2}}{3}-0)+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186179672 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179527 :question/id #uuid "2e6103cc-7be6-5eb6-ab5a-aa5aff3fa423" :question/math-academy-id "e-6319"} :knowledge-point/id $$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y+R(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}{e}^{y+z}\,\text{d}x+{e}^{x+z}\,\text{d}y+{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186536874 :question/id #uuid "b7927a26-b99a-5854-aa75-916116f0bbc7" :question/math-academy-id "q-125411"} {:db/id 17592186051070} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid vector-valued functions share a fundamental connection with line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y.$

Consider a vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with components $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j
$$

Now suppose that $C$ is a smooth curve on $\mathbb R^2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].
$$

Then, we can write the line integral of $\mathbf F$ along $C$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y
$$

An analogous result holds for vector fields on $\mathbb R^3.$ That is, 

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z
$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b4ca8cae-81df-5c55-90ac-839b063e78a6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5837 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4246c091-bba6-587e-8d43-72e5c01a1e08" :step/math-academy-id 35769 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180492}}] :activity/title "Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179857} {:db/id 17592186180501 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180722 :tutorial/content "Line integrals of vector-valued functions share a fundamental connection with line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y.$

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the section of the curve $y=-\sqrt{x}$ from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t)=t\,i-\sqrt{t}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 4.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=-\sqrt{t}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =t\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{8}{3} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t-\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2})\text{d}t+\frac{8}{3} \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{t}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{0}^{4}+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{4}^{3/2}}{3}-0)+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =8\end{aligned}

"a5bd2d24-7148-5ea0-938f-3c79b0f3f1dd" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Inverse of a Radical Function"}] :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{x}$." :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{x}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{y}
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= 1 - \frac{1}{3}\sqrt{y} \\
\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{y} &= 1 - x \\
\sqrt{y} &= 3(1 - x) \\
(\sqrt{y})^{2} &= (3(1 - x))^{2} \\
y &= 9(1 - x)^{2} \\
y &= 9(x - 1)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = 9(x - 1)^2
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are

$$
x \geq 0, \qquad f(x) \leq 1
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of $f^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x \leq 1, \qquad f^{-1}(x) \geq 0
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048784} {:db/id 17592186049461} {:db/id 17592186050639} {:db/id 17592186050802} {:db/id 17592186050850} {:db/id 17592186193002 :question/id #uuid "126761f9-7e00-5c24-882a-62bc8d1aaf11" :question/math-academy-id "q-148289"} {:db/id 17592186193012 :question/id #uuid "9ab37261-be43-5c11-815a-a3fe3812c90c" :question/math-academy-id "q-148443"} {:db/id 17592186192698 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192403 :question/id #uuid "8f01f2b7-13d5-58d3-8e2e-9f6804993094" :question/math-academy-id "e-10457"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "65cc2d11-c785-538a-a64d-5d3349040676" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193003 :question/id #uuid "d170561d-a12f-5a5e-8c7d-c28c8d751c38" :question/math-academy-id "q-148290"} {:db/id 17592186193004 :question/id #uuid "d7273791-5c15-5ed2-bbfc-be332cc50285" :question/math-academy-id "q-148291"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Inverse of a Radical Function Containing a Linear Argument"} {:db/id 17592186192403 :question/id #uuid "8f01f2b7-13d5-58d3-8e2e-9f6804993094" :question/math-academy-id "e-10457" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186192698 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "65cc2d11-c785-538a-a64d-5d3349040676" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Inverse of a Radical Function Containing a Linear Argument"}] :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{5}\sqrt{4x + 1}$." :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = \dfrac{1}{5}\sqrt{4x + 1}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{1}{5}\sqrt{4y + 1}
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{1}{5}\sqrt{4y + 1} \\
\sqrt{4y + 1} &= 5x \\
(\sqrt{4y + 1})^{2} &= (5x)^{2} \\
4y + 1 &= 25x^{2} \\
4y &= 25x^{2} - 1 \\
y &= \frac{1}{4}(25x^{2} - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(25x^2 - 1\right)
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are given by

$$
x \geq -\dfrac14, \qquad f(x) \geq 0
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of $f^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x \geq 0, \qquad f^{-1}(x) \geq -\dfrac14
$$"} {:db/id 17592186193003 :question/id #uuid "d170561d-a12f-5a5e-8c7d-c28c8d751c38" :question/math-academy-id "q-148290"} {:db/id 17592186193004 :question/id #uuid "d7273791-5c15-5ed2-bbfc-be332cc50285" :question/math-academy-id "q-148291"} {:db/id 17592186192699 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192404 :question/id #uuid "8760afc0-a7fb-5398-a585-c5559c9d1bb2" :question/math-academy-id "e-10458"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "10be7535-989f-5706-964e-06c02251d1f5" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193005 :question/id #uuid "8daf7d2c-3a2d-5092-9886-7a2423ea3543" :question/math-academy-id "q-148292"} {:db/id 17592186193006 :question/id #uuid "bc94d4e7-93a3-5a1e-9da3-04fab70d671c" :question/math-academy-id "q-148293"}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining an Unknown Value Given the Inverse of a Radical Function"} {:db/id 17592186192404 :question/id #uuid "8760afc0-a7fb-5398-a585-c5559c9d1bb2" :question/math-academy-id "e-10458" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186192699 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "10be7535-989f-5706-964e-06c02251d1f5" :knowledge-point/title "Determining an Unknown Value Given the Inverse of a Radical Function"}] :question/problem "The function $f(x) = 3\sqrt{x + k} - 2$ has an inverse function given by $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{9}(x + 2)^2 + 3$. What is the value of $k$?" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = 3\sqrt{x+k} - 2
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = 3\sqrt{y + k} - 2
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= 3\sqrt{y + k} - 2 \\
3\sqrt{y + k} &= x + 2 \\
\sqrt{y + k} &= \frac{1}{3}(x + 2) \\
(\sqrt{y + k})^{2} &= (\frac{1}{3}(x + 2))^{2} \\
y + k &= \frac{1}{9}(x + 2)^{2} \\
y &= \frac{1}{9}(x + 2)^{2} - k
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{9}(x + 2)^2 - k
$$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that

$$
-k = 3 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad k = -3
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are given by

$$
x \geq 3, \qquad f(x) \geq -2
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of $f^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x \geq -2, \qquad f^{-1}(x) \geq3
$$"} {:db/id 17592186193005 :question/id #uuid "8daf7d2c-3a2d-5092-9886-7a2423ea3543" :question/math-academy-id "q-148292"} {:db/id 17592186193006 :question/id #uuid "bc94d4e7-93a3-5a1e-9da3-04fab70d671c" :question/math-academy-id "q-148293"} {:db/id 17592186192707 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192415 :question/id #uuid "f689c3e3-9bb9-5e1e-b69a-b691373fdee0" :question/math-academy-id "e-10496"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fe915c05-2906-5873-8fd5-f364816f83bb" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050672} {:db/id 17592186050953}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193001 :question/id #uuid "d7546f9b-e164-5363-aa15-2d4ef97c5e2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-148288"} {:db/id 17592186193013 :question/id #uuid "f4c1cf18-a880-5282-8283-771dcb962b4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-148452"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Inverse of a Reciprocal Radical Function"} {:db/id 17592186192415 :question/id #uuid "f689c3e3-9bb9-5e1e-b69a-b691373fdee0" :question/math-academy-id "e-10496" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186192707 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fe915c05-2906-5873-8fd5-f364816f83bb" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Inverse of a Reciprocal Radical Function"}] :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt[3]{x}} + 1$." :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt[3]{x}} + 1
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt[3]{y}} + 1
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{3}{\sqrt[3]{y}} + 1 \\
x - 1 &= \frac{3}{\sqrt[3]{y}} \\
\frac{1}{x - 1} &= \frac{\sqrt[3]{y}}{3} \\
\sqrt[3]{y} &= \frac{3}{x - 1} \\
(\sqrt[3]{y})^{3} &= (\frac{3}{x - 1})^{3} \\
y &= (27)/((x - 1)^{3})
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{27}{(x - 1)^3}
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are

$$
x\neq 0, \qquad f(x)\neq 1
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of $f^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x\neq 1, \qquad f(x)\neq 0
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050672} {:db/id 17592186050953} {:db/id 17592186193001 :question/id #uuid "d7546f9b-e164-5363-aa15-2d4ef97c5e2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-148288" :knowledge-point/_questions For example, let's consider the following radical function:

$$
f(x) = 3\sqrt{x} + 2
$$

To compute the inverse of $f(x)$, we follow the usual four steps:

**Step 1:** First, we replace $f(x)$ with $y$:

$$
y = 3\sqrt{x} + 2
$$

**Step 2:** Then, we swap $x$ and $y$:

$$
x = 3\sqrt{y} + 2
$$

**Step 3:** Next, we solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= 3\sqrt{y} + 2 \\
3\sqrt{y} &= x - 2 \\
\sqrt{y} &= \frac{1}{3}(x - 2) \\
(\sqrt{y})^{2} &= (\frac{1}{3}(x - 2))^{2} \\
y &= \frac{1}{9}(x - 2)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4:** Finally, we replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x)$:

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{9}(x - 2)^2
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are

$$
x \geq 0, \qquad f(x) \geq 2
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of $f^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x \geq 2, \qquad f^{-1}(x) \geq 0
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "24753060-4992-520a-b948-f4e049858666" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6511 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f7338843-a969-5972-9416-842835e163e7" :step/math-academy-id :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we might need to use more than one rule of exponents to simplify an expression. First, let's remind ourselves of all of the rules of exponents.

- Radicals as fractional exponents: $\sqrt[n]{x} = x^{1/n}$

- The product rule: $a^n \cdot a^m = a^{n+m}$

- The quotient rule: $\dfrac{a^n}{a^m} = a^{n-m}$

- The power rule: $\left( a^m \right)^n = a^{mn}$

- The power of product rule: $(ab)^n = a^nb^n$

- The power of quotient rule: $\left(\dfrac a b \right)^n = \dfrac{a^n}{b^n}$

As an example, let's simplify the following expression:

$$
\left(u^2 v\right)^3
$$

We start by using the power of product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({u}^{2}v)}^{3}={({u}^{2})}^{3}\cdot {v}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({u}^{2})}^{3}\cdot {v}^{3} & = \\ {u}^{(2\cdot 3)}\cdot {v}^{3} & = \\ {u}^{6}\cdot {v}^{3} & = \\ {u}^{6}{v}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "13b1c64a-c868-5824-919e-c3a665bb4a96" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1485 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ff971efe-57b1-5d6a-a9d6-53728830ae56" :step/math-academy-id "73248b69-f18a-503e-b712-b3f56ae6841a" :step/math-academy-id 3569} {:db/id 17592186111601 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111904 :tutorial/content "To simplify the expression $x\cdot \sqrt[3]{x^2},$ we first rewrite the radical as a fractional exponent:

$$
x \cdot \sqrt[3]{x^2} = x \cdot \left( x^2 \right)^{1/3}
$$

Now, we apply the power rule for exponents:

$$
x \cdot \left( x^2 \right)^{1/3} = x \cdot x^{2(1/3)} = x \cdot x^{2/3}
$$

Then, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot {x}^{2/3} & = \\ {x}^{1+2/3} & = \\ {x}^{5/3} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we express the result as a radical:

$$
x^{5/3} = \sqrt[3]{x^5}
$$

Notice that, by combining the radicals as fractional exponents and power rules, we get the following formula:

$$
\sqrt[n]{x^m} = x^{m/n}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "91debf57-af23-518b-b432-ea04beccc17a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6221 :tutorial/title "Rules of Exponents and Radicals"} :step/id #uuid "d8d59c7e-2b45-5493-a09c-f4211a690c16" :step/math-academy-id 37772 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111597}}] :activity/title "Combining the Rules of Exponents With Algebraic Expressions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186110813} {:db/id 17592186111594 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111824 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we might need to use more than one rule of exponents to simplify an expression.
