</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=4Ax-5b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)={y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y)=2y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=2{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=4Ax-5b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}=4{\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-5{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=4{x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot 4{x}_{j} \\  & =8{y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $8$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=8y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =8y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =8(4Ax-5b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =8(4[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =8([\begin{aligned}16 \\ -16\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 15\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}208 \\ -248\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 832 \\ 0 & -992\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186542179 :question/id #uuid "a276eb8e-dc20-5069-8231-5e2d2d2a281a" :question/math-academy-id "q-269429" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5e1e29d1-1888-52aa-8dc6-4b2845f73611" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9" :db/id 17592186541611}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541611} :answer-field/id #uuid "5fa668de-a737-5f91-800a-6c4b031f88c5" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186542015} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33107365-8d72-59e7-84e4-fb7248465cbf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186541529}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541529} :answer-field/id #uuid "fd131918-eda5-51aa-9124-e861cbcfd218" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186542109}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 2}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b),$ where

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]?$

<table cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="70px" rowspan="2" width="30px">
${∇}_{A}=\,\,$
</td>
<td align="center" height="35px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">$9$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="35px"></td>
<td align="center">$-6$</td>
<td align="center">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)=y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}={y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =(Ax-b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 \\ -6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer-field/id #uuid "a792c03a-20d1-502a-87d8-51c51290a0f7" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186203428} {:answer-field/id #uuid "d8fb804b-e34c-5518-b27d-f7e1b108969b" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186203429} {:answer-field/id #uuid "f24f27c1-d129-569d-91c5-ec978eca7083" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186203430} {:answer-field/id #uuid "1b648609-00c6-5d8f-b7a0-5619dddfcab1" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186203431} {:activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186205011} :activity/id #uuid "f13da08f-0333-5cf7-8f52-a79e6bf0ebd6" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048550 :topic/id #uuid "a9165535-d837-58b0-9784-39a400db9d86" :topic/math-academy-id 5869} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186205011 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205186 :tutorial/content "In previous lessons, we defined the gradient of a scalar-valued function with respect to a vector. In this lesson, we extend this idea to functions where the input is a *matrix* and the output is a scalar.

Suppose we have a function $f: \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} \to \mathbb{R}$ that maps a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ to a scalar value $f(A)$. Just like with vector inputs, we define the **gradient of $f$ with respect to $A$** as the matrix of partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to each individual entry of $A{:}$

![](images/0b/0b3ce184c982fe85eb25f79161431b7620227b96909d87998fa82efbb469423c.svg)

This gradient has the same shape as the matrix $A.$ It tells us how sensitive the output $f(A)$ is to changes in each element $a_{ij}$.

Let’s apply this to a concrete example. Suppose we define the function

$$
f(X) = \ln(\det(X))
$$

for a square matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$. Let's find the gradient of $f$ with respect to $X$ and evaluate it at a specific point.

First, we write the matrix $X$ as
![](images/67/67c8cc92409c6bd1595fda93c8711ce91a40d220526cc52ee9a8f4d3842f7354.svg)
Then, the determinant of $X$ is

$$
\det(X) = x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21}.
$$

So, the function becomes

$$
f(X) = \ln(x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21}).
$$

To find the gradient, we differentiate $f$ with respect to each element of $X.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{X}f(X) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{11}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{12}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{21}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{22}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{11}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{12}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{21}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{22}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}_{22}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}} & -\frac{{x}_{21}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}} \\ -\frac{{x}_{12}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}} & \frac{{x}_{11}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{22} & -{x}_{21} \\ -{x}_{12} & {x}_{11}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{det(X)}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{22} & -{x}_{21} \\ -{x}_{12} & {x}_{11}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, suppose we wish to evaluate this gradient at
![](images/93/93200d9d52e6a58a52e4b9f65db6bc13ded0c6e17dbb8fc0381ae40081932ff9.svg)
First, we compute the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(X) & =3\cdot (-2)-1\cdot 5 \\  & =-6-5 \\  & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our values into our gradient. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{X}f(X) & =-\frac{1}{11}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{11}[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This result tells us how the scalar output $f(X) = \ln(\det(X))$ would change with respect to small changes in each entry of the matrix $X$. Each element in the gradient matrix captures that local rate of change." :tutorial/id #uuid "4ace4da9-e2b2-56f1-b064-78e25344a30e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12175 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "51d89ff0-2e51-5813-be29-4f290760f1f7" :step/math-academy-id 450917 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205012}} {:db/id 17592186205012 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204079 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203857 :question/id #uuid "ca1002c8-c615-5f7b-8876-82cf87c8864f" :question/math-academy-id "e-17349"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c676a83b-f3d4-579b-ab54-de2104552e8f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050484}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204564} {:db/id 17592186204572} {:db/id 17592186533992} {:db/id 17592186533993} {:db/id 17592186534003}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Gradient of a Function With Respect to a Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "5682316e-09ab-5709-825d-abbce84fe179" :step/math-academy-id 450918 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205013}} {:db/id 17592186205013 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205192 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a scalar-valued function defined by

$$
f = \mathbf{y}^T A \mathbf{x},
$$

where $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$.

We want to compute the gradient of $f$ with respect to the matrix $A$. The result turns out to be

$$
\nabla_A f = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T.
$$

Let’s verify this by working component-wise. 

First, note that we can write the product $\mathbf y^T A \mathbf x$ as a double summation as follows:

$$
f = \mathbf y^T A \mathbf x = \sum_{k=1}^m \sum_{l=1}^n y_k A_{kl} x_l.
$$

In a previous lesson, we saw how to do this for $\mathbf x^T A \mathbf x$. The idea here is similar.

Now, we differentiate this summation with respect to $A_{ij}{:}$

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial A_{ij}} 
= \frac{\partial}{\partial A_{ij}} \left( \sum_{k=1}^m \sum_{l=1}^n y_k A_{kl} x_l \right)
$$

Since only the term where $k = i$ and $l = j$ depends on $A_{ij}$, all other terms vanish. So, we get

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial A_{ij}} 
= y_i x_j.
$$

This tells us that the entry in the $i$th row and $j$th column of the gradient matrix is $y_i x_j$. Hence, the full gradient matrix is

$$
\nabla_A f = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T.
$$

This result is an example of an outer product. The gradient of $\mathbf{y}^T A \mathbf{x}$ with respect to the matrix $A$ is given by multiplying the column vector $\mathbf{y}$ by the row vector $\mathbf{x}^T$, resulting in a matrix of the same shape as $A$.

Let’s look at a few examples to see this in action." :tutorial/id #uuid "957b6db8-152d-50d1-9685-1b280888ce3d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12388 :tutorial/title "Component-Wise Differentiation"} :step/id #uuid "40001fda-db52-5314-a824-eba6f4cc9e69" :step/math-academy-id 450921 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205014}} {:db/id 17592186205014 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204080 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203871 :question/id #uuid "5aa67862-6f7a-57ac-9473-d039fc4bfec4" :question/math-academy-id "e-17951"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "35dc17b6-1c82-55ec-9657-20f2850794e5" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204578} {:db/id 17592186204584} {:db/id 17592186533986} {:db/id 17592186534000} {:db/id 17592186534008} {:db/id 17592186534029} {:db/id 17592186534034} {:db/id 17592186542190}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Gradient of a Function Component-Wise"} :step/id #uuid "ad3cf801-8dd4-5f9a-b7ca-588e439c66cc" :step/math-academy-id 450922 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205015}} {:db/id 17592186205015 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205195 :tutorial/content "When working with scalar-valued functions defined on matrices, it's often helpful to compute gradients using component-wise differentiation and the chain rule. This approach breaks down the computation into simpler intermediate steps and allows us to clearly see the dependencies.

Consider a *scalar* function $L(\mathbf A),$ defined as

$$
L(\mathbf{A}) = \frac{1}{2} \left( \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \right)^T \left( \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \right)
$$

where $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}$, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$, and $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^2.$

Suppose we want to compute the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L$, which is a matrix of the same shape as $\mathbf{A}$. The entry in the $i$th row and $j$th column of the gradient matrix is given by 

$$
\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}.
$$

To simplify the differentiation, we define $\mathbf y \in\mathbb R^{2\times 1}$ as 
![](images/d1/d14a8e7752fdc2f20c9c325c5a0076d79a86ccd2a0c46d6b353ce53c3f1561d7.svg)

Then, we can write $L$ in terms of $\mathbf y$ as 

$$
L = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

To compute $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}$, we apply the multivariable chain rule:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}} = \sum_{k=1}^2 \frac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} \cdot \frac{\partial y_k}{\partial a_{ij}}
$$

Note that the summation is from $k=1$ to $k=2$ because $\mathbf y$ has two components, and we're differentiating with respect to each of them.

Now, let's analyze the two factors of the product that appear in this summation.

- We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{y}L & ={∇}_{y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2y \\  & =y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} = y_k.
$$

- Writing $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}$ in component form

$$
y_i = \sum_{j=1}^3 a_{ij} x_j - b_i,
$$

we have
![](images/76/761731b884eee7282e01bda6964861fc8f3d4a3a44bfec09fda478170982b56a.svg)
Only the $k$th row of $\mathbf{A}$ affects $y_k$.

Putting our two results together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j},\end{aligned}
$$

because all terms vanish except the one where $k=i$.

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T.
$$

In the next example, we will use this formula to compute the gradient for specific vectors." :tutorial/id #uuid "2a8a781f-98de-5bf4-8f02-80c10f3211b3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12479 :tutorial/title "Differentiation Using the Multivariable Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "da5331f6-b68e-5fed-80d1-95b4e0971765" :step/math-academy-id 450925 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205016}} {:db/id 17592186205016 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204081 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203866 :question/id #uuid "429a6a34-2fe5-5c09-9b74-e4b650209007" :question/math-academy-id "e-17870"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ef7b2139-06eb-5584-a267-d9fbc9b5d041" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050031}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204583} {:db/id 17592186204585} {:db/id 17592186534022} {:db/id 17592186534073} {:db/id 17592186534080} {:db/id 17592186534082} {:db/id 17592186542139} {:db/id 17592186542179}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Chain Rule to Calculate Gradients"} :step/id #uuid "0dbe27ec-63c8-5d16-a0de-f9deb9e9f3e8" :step/math-academy-id 450926}] :activity/title "Matrix Gradients" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186204182} {:db/id 17592186205011 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205186 :tutorial/content "In previous lessons, we defined the gradient of a scalar-valued function with respect to a vector. ![](images/67/67c8cc92409c6bd1595fda93c8711ce91a40d220526cc52ee9a8f4d3842f7354.svg)
Then, the determinant of $X$ is

$$
\det(X) = x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21}.
$$

So, the function becomes

$$
f(X) = \ln(x_{11}x_{22} - x_{12}x_{21}).
$$

To find the gradient, we differentiate $f$ with respect to each element of $X.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{X}f(X) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{11}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{12}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{21}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{22}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{11}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{12}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{21}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21})) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{22}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}_{22}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}} & -\frac{{x}_{21}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}} \\ -\frac{{x}_{12}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}} & \frac{{x}_{11}}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}_{11}{x}_{22}-{x}_{12}{x}_{21}}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{22} & -{x}_{21} \\ -{x}_{12} & {x}_{11}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{det(X)}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{22} & -{x}_{21} \\ -{x}_{12} & {x}_{11}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, suppose we wish to evaluate this gradient at
![](images/93/93200d9d52e6a58a52e4b9f65db6bc13ded0c6e17dbb8fc0381ae40081932ff9.svg)
First, we compute the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(X) & =3\cdot (-2)-1\cdot 5 \\  & =-6-5 \\  & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our values into our gradient. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{X}f(X) & =-\frac{1}{11}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{11}[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This result tells us how the scalar output $f(X) = \ln(\det(X))$ would change with respect to small changes in each entry of the matrix $X$. Each element in the gradient matrix captures that local rate of change." :tutorial/id #uuid "4ace4da9-e2b2-56f1-b064-78e25344a30e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12175 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186205012 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204079 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203857 :question/id #uuid "ca1002c8-c615-5f7b-8876-82cf87c8864f" :question/math-academy-id "e-17349"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c676a83b-f3d4-579b-ab54-de2104552e8f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050484}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204564} {:db/id 17592186204572} {:db/id 17592186533992} {:db/id 17592186533993} {:db/id 17592186534003}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Gradient of a Function With Respect to a Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "5682316e-09ab-5709-825d-abbce84fe179" :step/math-academy-id 450918 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205013}} {:db/id 17592186205013 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205192 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a scalar-valued function defined by

$$
f = \mathbf{y}^T A \mathbf{x},
$$

where $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$.

We want to compute the gradient of $f$ with respect to the matrix $A$. The result turns out to be

$$
\nabla_A f = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T.
$$

Let’s verify this by working component-wise. 

First, note that we can write the product $\mathbf y^T A \mathbf x$ as a double summation as follows:

$$
f = \mathbf y^T A \mathbf x = \sum_{k=1}^m \sum_{l=1}^n y_k A_{kl} x_l.
$$

In a previous lesson, we saw how to do this for $\mathbf x^T A \mathbf x$. The idea here is similar.

Now, we differentiate this summation with respect to $A_{ij}{:}$

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial A_{ij}} 
= \frac{\partial}{\partial A_{ij}} \left( \sum_{k=1}^m \sum_{l=1}^n y_k A_{kl} x_l \right)
$$

Since only the term where $k = i$ and $l = j$ depends on $A_{ij}$, all other terms vanish. So, we get

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial A_{ij}} 
= y_i x_j.
$$

This tells us that the entry in the $i$th row and $j$th column of the gradient matrix is $y_i x_j$. Hence, the full gradient matrix is

$$
\nabla_A f = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T.
$$

This result is an example of an outer product. The gradient of $\mathbf{y}^T A \mathbf{x}$ with respect to the matrix $A$ is given by multiplying the column vector $\mathbf{y}$ by the row vector $\mathbf{x}^T$, resulting in a matrix of the same shape as $A$.

Let’s look at a few examples to see this in action." :tutorial/id #uuid "957b6db8-152d-50d1-9685-1b280888ce3d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12388 :tutorial/title "Component-Wise Differentiation"} :step/id #uuid "40001fda-db52-5314-a824-eba6f4cc9e69" :step/math-academy-id 450921 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205014}} {:db/id 17592186205192 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a scalar-valued function defined by

This approach breaks down the computation into simpler intermediate steps and allows us to clearly see the dependencies.

Consider a *scalar* function $L(\mathbf A),$ defined as

$$
L(\mathbf{A}) = \frac{1}{2} \left( \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \right)^T \left( \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \right)
$$

where $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}$, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$, and $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^2.$

Suppose we want to compute the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L$, which is a matrix of the same shape as $\mathbf{A}$. The entry in the $i$th row and $j$th column of the gradient matrix is given by 

$$
\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}.
$$

To simplify the differentiation, we define $\mathbf y \in\mathbb R^{2\times 1}$ as 
![](images/d1/d14a8e7752fdc2f20c9c325c5a0076d79a86ccd2a0c46d6b353ce53c3f1561d7.svg)

Then, we can write $L$ in terms of $\mathbf y$ as 

$$
L = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

To compute $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}}$, we apply the multivariable chain rule:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a_{ij}} = \sum_{k=1}^2 \frac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} \cdot \frac{\partial y_k}{\partial a_{ij}}
$$

Note that the summation is from $k=1$ to $k=2$ because $\mathbf y$ has two components, and we're differentiating with respect to each of them.

Now, let's analyze the two factors of the product that appear in this summation.

- We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{y}L & ={∇}_{y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2y \\  & =y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_k} = y_k.
$$

- Writing $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}$ in component form

$$
y_i = \sum_{j=1}^3 a_{ij} x_j - b_i,
$$

we have
![](images/76/761731b884eee7282e01bda6964861fc8f3d4a3a44bfec09fda478170982b56a.svg)
Only the $k$th row of $\mathbf{A}$ affects $y_k$.

Putting our two results together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j},\end{aligned}
$$

because all terms vanish except the one where $k=i$.

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{A}} L = \mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{x}^T.
$$

In the next example, we will use this formula to compute the gradient for specific vectors." :tutorial/id #uuid "2a8a781f-98de-5bf4-8f02-80c10f3211b3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12479 :tutorial/title "Differentiation Using the Multivariable Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "da5331f6-b68e-5fed-80d1-95b4e0971765" :step/math-academy-id 450925 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205016}} {:db/id 17592186205195 :tutorial/content "When working with scalar-valued functions defined on matrices, it's often helpful to compute gradients using component-wise differentiation and the chain rule. $$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=4Ax-5b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)={y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y)=2y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=2{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=4Ax-5b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}=4{\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-5{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=4{x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot 4{x}_{j} \\  & =8{y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $8$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=8y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y$ and

$$

$$

$$
y = ax^2+bx+c
$$

with $a=1>0$, $b=4$, and $c=6$.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the parabola opens upward. Consequently, there is no maximum output, and the vertex corresponds to the minimum output.

The $x$-coordinate of the vertex is given by

$$
x= -\dfrac{b}{2a} = -\dfrac{4}{2 \cdot 1} = -2
$$

Now, we substitute $x=-2$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= x^{2} + 4x + 6 \\
&= (-2)^{2} + 4(-2) + 6 \\
&= 4 - 8 + 6 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(-2,2)$, and the range of the function is $[2,\infty)$.

$$
y = a(x-x_1)(x-x_2)
$$

with

$$
a = -\dfrac{1}{2} < 0
$$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are $x_1=-3$ and $x_2=1$, and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{x_{1} + x_{2}}{2} = \frac{-3 + 1}{2} =-1
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=-1$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= -\frac{1}{2}(x + 3)(x - 1) \\
&=-\frac{1}{2}(-1 + 3)(-1 - 1) \\
&=-\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot (-2) \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(-1,2)$, and the range of the function is $(-\infty,2]$.

Regardless of whether the equation is written in standard form,

$$
y = ax^2 + bx + c
$$

vertex form,

$$
y = a(x-h)^2 + k
$$

or factored form,

$$

$$

it opens upwards if the leading coefficient $a$ is positive and downwards if $a$ is negative.

Now, consider a parabola that opens upwards ($a>0$). In this case, the minimum output corresponds to the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, while there is no maximum output. Therefore, if the vertex is $(h,k)$, then the range is

$$
y \geq k
$$

For example, in the graph below, the $y$-value of the vertex is $y=-2$, so the range of the function is

$$

"e-21835" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186221443 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "12ff3452-19b6-566a-8b39-ad880dee8858" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Effects of the Horizontal Scaling on Coefficients"}] :question/problem "Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in [-L,L)$ to $x \in \mathbb R.$ 
Given that $L=2$ and $f(x) = \cosh{(x+1)}$, find the $4$th cosine and the $4$th sine coefficients." :question/worked-solution "Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k \neq 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s) = f\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)
$$

must have a period of $2L \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{L} = 2\pi.$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s) = f\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x){:}$

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
a_n\cos\bigg(\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x}\bigg)+
b_n\sin\bigg(\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x}\bigg)
$$

Therefore, $4$th cosine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, $4$th sine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=2$ and $f(x)=\cosh(x+1),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)\,\text{d}x, \\ {b}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186222018 :question/id #uuid "ce16504e-7202-575c-a3a2-02f06481c9e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-340836"} {:db/id 17592186222028 :question/id #uuid :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186221444 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cb301102-1a82-5a81-bb11-b9fc56cd1dc7" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Constant Term For the Fourier Series"}] :question/problem "$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{2}x\right)+b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{2}x\right)
$$

Let $F(x)=3x^2-4x+1$ for $x\in[-2,2).$ The Fourier series of the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of $a_0.$" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the constant term is given by

$$
a_0=\frac{1}{L}\int_{-L}^{L} f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and $f(x)=3x^2-4x+1$ for $x \in [-2,2).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(3{x}^{2}-4x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x]}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(({2}^{3}-2\cdot {2}^{2}+2)-((-2)^{3}-2\cdot (-2)^{2}+(-2))) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2-(-18)) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 6382} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222376 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222514 :tutorial/content "When a function has period $2L$ (instead of $2\pi$), the "usual" Fourier formulas still work, but the sine and cosine inputs must be rescaled so that each term completes an integer number of oscillations over one period. 

We do this by converting the $2L$-periodic function into a $2\pi$-periodic one using a change of variables.

Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in[-L,L)$ to $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
To use the standard $2\pi$-period Fourier formulas, define

$$
s=\frac{\pi}{L}x
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g(s)=f\!\left(\frac{L}{\pi}s\right).
$$

Then $g$ is $2\pi$-periodic.

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $g$, the Fourier series is

$$
g(s)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl(a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns)\bigr),
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,ds, \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1, \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,ds,\,n\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute $g(s)=f\!\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)$ and $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$.
First, for $a_n{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,ds \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f\,(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)cos\,(n\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,d\,(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Coefficients $b_n$ (for $n \geq 1$) and $a_0$ can be found similarly.

To summarize, the Fourier series of $f$ is

$$
f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(a_n\cos\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\right),
$$

where the coefficients are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,dx \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)sin\,(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,dx,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's see some concrete examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "5bb98db0-8e34-5cf2-8911-56a6971740ab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14681 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{3}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{3}x)
$$

Let $F(x)=6x+1$ for $x\in [-3,3).$ The Fourier series of the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${b}_{5}.$

${b}_{5}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the sine coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=3$ and $f(x)=6x+1$ for $x\in (-3,3).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{5}=\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(6x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=6x+1\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=6 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{3}{5\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{5} & =\frac{1}{3}(uv\,{|}_{-3}^{3}-{\int }_{-3}^{3}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-\frac{3}{5\pi }{[(6x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{3}+\frac{18}{5\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\pi }(-{[(6x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{3}+6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\pi }(-((6(3)+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi )-(6(-3)+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-5\pi ))+\frac{18}{5\pi }{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\pi }(36+\frac{18}{5\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-5\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\pi }\cdot 36 \\  & =\frac{36}{5\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2f23af18-6fc6-51a2-9ae3-01f862c5c75a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186525086}} {:db/id 17592186525086 :step/content {:db/id 17592186372791 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7b5be5de-ac24-5096-b91d-e0e0ff8e3983" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30" :db/id 17592186372793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186372793} :answer-field/id #uuid "3cb42d37-67e0-5792-9f61-4d038363d4ad" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186372792}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7cfbfb37-8e3e-5c3d-8267-64ce726f2c24" :question/math-academy-id "q-341788" :question/problem "$$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=9$ and $f(x)=3x+\frac{1}{2}$ for $x\in [-9,9).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{9}{\int }_{-9}^{9}(3x+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x]}_{-9}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}((\frac{3}{2}\cdot {9}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9)-(\frac{3}{2}\cdot (-9)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-9))) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(126-117) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

The Fourier series of the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function 

$$

$$

${a}_{2}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=3.$ Also, $f(x)=1$ for $x\in [0,3)$ and $f(x)=-4$ for $x\in [-3,0).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{3}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{0}(-4)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2\pi }{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{0}+\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2\pi }{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}x)]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi ))+\frac{1}{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cf1e87c7-8f9a-5050-a189-bceb0d6f5b0e"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "93a95dfd-61c1-5b85-ad7a-7edfc0702959" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186524618}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186524618} :answer-field/id #uuid "79cdb461-38af-5784-a292-e83653dfa433" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186524895} {:answer/id #uuid "93a95dfd-61c1-5b85-ad7a-7edfc0702959" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186524618} {:db/id 17592186048726 :topic/difficulty 0.9613223291088446 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428517 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $$

$$

$$

and $f(x)={x}^{21}-16{x}^{19}+6x-3$, find $f(A).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4-\lambda  & 12 \\ 0 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda ) \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-16\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

<td align="left" colspan="7" height="20" width="20">$\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{21}\,-\,16{x}^{19}\,+\,6x\,\,-\,\,3\phantom{|}}$</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">${x}^{21}$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$-$</td>

</tr>

<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$6x$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$-$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$3$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(6x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{19}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(6A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(6A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(6A-3I) \\  & =6A-3I \\  & =6\begin{bmatrix}4 & 12 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}24 & 72 \\ 0 & -24\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}21 & 72 \\ 0 & -27\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186392147 :question/id #uuid "df379c8f-bbed-5154-8e34-f7aedf45ba74" :question/math-academy-id "q-37844" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124538 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "787173e1-f957-5ff0-9d14-a6ccb11de1d8" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33d95a80-3f16-57c4-aa0e-d7a0b263509f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}11 & 8 \\ -24 & -16\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186392149} {:answer/id #uuid "7ade6fcc-fefb-5c26-9596-732bb7e6456e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}11 & -24 \\ 8 & -16\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186392150} {:answer/id #uuid "ac8f35b7-246a-5615-af02-78cc8b431c3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}25 & 16 \\ -48 & -31\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186392151} {:answer/id #uuid "bf93252a-5145-5f3e-a1e5-9eed34f606e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}16 & -25 \\ 18 & -42\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186392152} {:answer/id #uuid "46d0fa8b-a3e4-5c81-b011-49838b661fc3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}40 & 24 \\ -70 & -44\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186392153}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ac8f35b7-246a-5615-af02-78cc8b431c3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}25 & 16 \\ -48 & -31\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186392151} :answer-field/id #uuid "5a7442f8-2e08-50f7-921a-87fb338cdbdb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186392148}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Given the matrix
$\,A=\begin{bmatrix}14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14\end{bmatrix}$
and $f(x)={x}^{12}-4{x}^{10}+{x}^{3}-2x-3$, find $f(A).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}14-\lambda  & 8 \\ -24 & -14-\lambda \end{vmatrix} \\  & =(14-\lambda )(-14-\lambda )+192 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,{x}^{10}$ | $+$ | $x$ |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-4\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{12}-4{x}^{10}+{x}^{3}-2x-3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{12}$ | $\,\,\,\,-$ | $\,\,\,\,4{x}^{10}$ |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  | ${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ | $-\,\,$ | $\,\,2x$ | $\,\,\,\,\,-$ | $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$ |
|  |  |  |  | ${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ | $-\,\,$ | $\,\,4x$ |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  |  | $\,\,2x$ | $\,\,\,\,\,-$ | $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,3$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(2x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{10}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(2A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(2A-3I) \\  & =2A-3I \\  & =2\begin{bmatrix}14 & 8 \\ -24 & -14\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}28 & 16 \\ -48 & -28\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}25 & 16 \\ -48 & -31\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186392218 :question/id #uuid "6884fbdf-c141-559a-9c69-73ca1eb1083a" :question/math-academy-id "q-38727"} {:db/id 17592186392225 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2} &=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} &=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 1972} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125429 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125794 :tutorial/content "The characteristic equation of a square matrix $A$ is given by 

$$
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
$$

On the left-hand side of this equation, we have the expression 

$$
\det(A-\lambda I),
$$

 which we call the **characteristic polynomial** of the matrix $A.$

For instance, let's find the characteristic polynomial of the matrix ![](images/1d/1d6d0bdedbb25bbc41759e443cdc0f6a207ef5cbfa4761b05e1a1a2eda24cbec.svg)

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(C-\lambda I) \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & -9 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| \\  & =(-8-\lambda )\cdot (7-\lambda )-(-9)\cdot 6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "25396b96-19ec-592d-b1c4-3c6fa172ef08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3580 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9083e01a-4e57-589b-9b08-48ecc4af0075" :step/math-academy-id 20133 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125433}} {:db/id 17592186125430 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125795 :tutorial/content "The **Cayley-Hamilton theorem** states the following: 

*Let $A$ be an $\,n \!\times\! n$ matrix whose characteristic polynomial is* 

$$
p(\lambda) = \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) = (-1)^n\lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda + c_0.
$$

*Then, the matrix $A$ is a solution of the characteristic equation $p(\lambda) = 0$.* 

That is to say, if we substitute $A$ into the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$, taking $A^0 = I,$ then we have

$$
p(A) = (-1)^nA^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A + c_0I = O,
$$

where $O$ is the zero-matrix. 

For example, according to this theorem, for the matrix 
![](images/d2/d24f480293267a9ddc28b03626e7bde6f01bd62a136fed17f8580bf1ea34d776.svg)
whose characteristic polynomial is 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2 +\lambda -2,
$$

we have

$$
p(A) = A^2 +A -2I =O.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86101838-75af-5a3f-9dae-1e63a94c77a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3581 :tutorial/title "The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "7b3b4f95-8159-5533-bd80-db194716f75b" :tutorial/content "What conclusions can we make regarding the characteristic polynomial of the general $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/8e/8e26937ef1981804a548e92a4041bd8672cc75c7c5cc6efa0c0c2694c0736791.svg)

First, let's find the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \left|\begin{aligned}a-\lambda  & b \\ c & d-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| & =0 \\ (a-\lambda )(d-\lambda )-bc & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-(a+d)\lambda +(ad-bc) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the constant term is the determinant of the matrix: 

$$
\det(A) = ad-bc
$$

 

The coefficient of $\lambda$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$ taken with a negative sign. The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix $A$ is called the **trace** of $A,$ and we denote it as 

$$
\mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d.
$$

So, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A$, the characteristic polynomial is

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 -\mathrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A).
$$

**Note:** This result can be extended to the general case of $n \times n$ matrices. If $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then its characteristic polynomial takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{c}_{n-1}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{c}_{0} \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{{(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{n-1}}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{{det(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{0}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)\,\text{and}\,{c}_{0}=det(A).\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1c54b7a6-10ea-5c57-ad4e-245a308d4790" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3582 :tutorial/title "The Characteristic Polynomial for 2x2 Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "f3faf291-dd20-56c9-bc3d-8482113b6764" :step/math-academy-id 21546 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125430}} {:db/id 17592186125502 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125824 :tutorial/content "If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](images/0f/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. $$

*Then, the matrix $A$ is a solution of the characteristic equation $p(\lambda) = 0$.* 

That is to say, if we substitute $A$ into the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$, taking $A^0 = I,$ then we have

$$
p(A) = (-1)^nA^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A + c_0I = O,
$$

where $O$ is the zero-matrix. 

For example, according to this theorem, for the matrix 
![](images/d2/d24f480293267a9ddc28b03626e7bde6f01bd62a136fed17f8580bf1ea34d776.svg)
whose characteristic polynomial is 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2 +\lambda -2,
$$

we have

$$
p(A) = A^2 +A -2I =O.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86101838-75af-5a3f-9dae-1e63a94c77a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3581 :tutorial/title "The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "7b3b4f95-8159-5533-bd80-db194716f75b" :step/math-academy-id 20134 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125432}} {:db/id 17592186125795 :tutorial/content "The **Cayley-Hamilton theorem** states the following:

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86101838-75af-5a3f-9dae-1e63a94c77a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3581 :tutorial/title "The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem"} {:db/id 17592186125432 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124537 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124346 :question/id #uuid "8e6d3017-d05d-5a2d-8043-c827e612476e" :question/math-academy-id "e-5511"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b2867571-c1ae-5ea0-b784-22f444c8db38" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125137} {:db/id 17592186125140} {:db/id 17592186272120} {:db/id 17592186272121} {:db/id 17592186351502} {:db/id 17592186351503} {:db/id 17592186351504} {:db/id 17592186351505} {:db/id 17592186354443} {:db/id 17592186354444} {:db/id 17592186354445} {:db/id 17592186430413}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Power of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Smaller Powers"} :step/id #uuid "1c6e6482-d051-50c1-b91d-40d9a95a380d" :step/math-academy-id 20136 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125431}} {:db/id 17592186125431 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124536 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124345 :question/id #uuid "c262f28d-bfd0-5c78-bce7-d2ae314052e1" :question/math-academy-id "e-5510"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "152243fa-e0a5-551d-92d9-b470789087c7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125097} {:db/id 17592186125098} {:db/id 17592186272126} {:db/id 17592186323940} {:db/id 17592186323945} {:db/id 17592186326708} {:db/id 17592186326811} {:db/id 17592186326812} {:db/id 17592186354446} {:db/id 17592186354447} {:db/id 17592186373778} {:db/id 17592186430412}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers"} :step/id #uuid "d9e0bce9-63bf-58e4-af9b-2bb5b5d8e03c" :step/math-academy-id 20135 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125502}} {:db/id 17592186125502 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125824 :tutorial/content "If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](images/0f/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this." :tutorial/id #uuid "769ceb10-1667-52b6-8a89-b4c7ca835276" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4448 :tutorial/title "Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem to Quickly Evaluate a Matrix Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "3167e19f-42e7-5fc7-8ee9-fb73a5fa3da3" :step/math-academy-id 27370 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125434}} {:db/id 17592186125796 :tutorial/content "What conclusions can we make regarding the characteristic polynomial of the general $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/8e/8e26937ef1981804a548e92a4041bd8672cc75c7c5cc6efa0c0c2694c0736791.svg)

First, let's find the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \left|\begin{aligned}a-\lambda  & b \\ c & d-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| & =0 \\ (a-\lambda )(d-\lambda )-bc & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-(a+d)\lambda +(ad-bc) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the constant term is the determinant of the matrix: 

$$
\det(A) = ad-bc
$$

 

The coefficient of $\lambda$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$ taken with a negative sign. The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix $A$ is called the **trace** of $A,$ and we denote it as 

$$
\mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d.
$$

So, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A$, the characteristic polynomial is

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 -\mathrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A).
$$

**Note:** This result can be extended to the general case of $n \times n$ matrices. If $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then its characteristic polynomial takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{c}_{n-1}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{c}_{0} \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{{(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{n-1}}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{{det(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{0}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)\,\text{and}\,{c}_{0}=det(A).\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1c54b7a6-10ea-5c57-ad4e-245a308d4790" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3582 :tutorial/title "The Characteristic Polynomial for 2x2 Matrices"} {:db/id 17592186125455 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124552 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124361 :question/id #uuid "95b44b17-b796-51eb-93dd-4ee4b2e5c3f2" :question/math-academy-id "e-5894"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "87febdb4-5f54-5aff-b84a-1b05359d6b57" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050376} {:db/id 17592186050669}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125139} {:db/id 17592186125141} {:db/id 17592186272119} {:db/id 17592186326707} {:db/id 17592186351499} {:db/id 17592186351500} {:db/id 17592186351501} {:db/id 17592186354441} {:db/id 17592186354442} {:db/id 17592186430411} {:db/id 17592186486439}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Sum and Product of Eigenvalues of a 2x2 Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "f3faf291-dd20-56c9-bc3d-8482113b6764" :step/math-academy-id 21546 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125430}} {:db/id 17592186125434 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124538 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124347 :question/id #uuid "ce724b3b-f440-5c1f-86a6-c50a54931233" :question/math-academy-id "e-5512"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "787173e1-f957-5ff0-9d14-a6ccb11de1d8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050117}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125096} {:db/id 17592186125106} {:db/id 17592186272142} {:db/id 17592186272144} {:db/id 17592186323938} {:db/id 17592186323939} {:db/id 17592186326709} {:db/id 17592186354448} {:db/id 17592186354451} {:db/id 17592186392147} {:db/id 17592186392218} {:db/id 17592186392225}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "0fed3d43-139d-505f-8482-70f3be0516d6" :step/math-academy-id 20138} {:db/id 17592186125824 :tutorial/content "If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. $$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+8I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+8I) & =O \\ A-7I+8{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{8}I-\frac{1}{8}A\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(A) & =O \\ {A}^{3}-{A}^{2}+3A-16I & =O \\ {A}^{3} & ={A}^{2}-3A+16I.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "864708dc-01cf-5025-81a5-3d649155dedc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186440842}} {:db/id 17592186440844 :step/content {:db/id 17592186326708 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28cc5ee2-6da9-52c1-a92b-8edb26634139" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{6}" :db/id 17592186324300} {:answer/id #uuid "47e93b3f-33d7-5090-b1fc-02844e927bff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{7}{6}" :db/id 17592186324553} {:answer/id #uuid "a44579f4-a9e4-53da-a506-9eefbb4bf2e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186325367} {:answer/id #uuid "bd8f6f17-d42e-553d-a74b-0e76268b5611" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186325601} {:answer/id #uuid "d1b95922-aad1-5b77-a0d0-e6a698ab713b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186325792}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186324300} :answer-field/id #uuid "36035083-9336-58a8-9968-10256743cb12" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326311}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "688a2834-9fcd-5275-97a0-97e7aaa1b79c" :question/math-academy-id "q-38704" :question/problem "Given that $\,A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+6I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+6I) & =O \\ A-8I+6{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 6{A}^{-1} & =8I-A \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{4}{3}I-\frac{1}{6}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{4}{3},$ $q=-\frac{1}{6}$ and

$$

$\,A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 12 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}$
and $f(x)={x}^{21}-16{x}^{19}+6x-3$, find $f(A).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned}

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\  & =7A-3I \\  & =7\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a1707eef-06e0-5503-8342-6b9421462ee5"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186486487} :activity/id #uuid "335bb2d0-e529-5cbe-ad74-695b640df1d6" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048726 :topic/id #uuid "b8f25367-71a5-50d2-9e6e-d239937a1fac" :topic/math-academy-id 1972} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186486472 :step/content {:db/id 17592186326811 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17bf09fd-3fd5-5fa9-bd7c-9bb8300133ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}I-\frac{1}{2}A-\frac{3}{2}{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186324178} {:answer/id #uuid "2196ad3b-dc18-575d-9ac5-f3e82f2cf1f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}I-\frac{1}{2}A-\frac{1}{2}{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186324248} {:answer/id #uuid "ae47339b-004d-5c20-8d9d-8aab1f4f98f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2I-A-2{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186325449} {:answer/id #uuid "bc9f773a-008b-571e-8538-a3402ba6e607" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}I-\frac{7}{2}A-\frac{1}{2}{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186325590} {:answer/id #uuid "d899671a-8147-5a25-9c47-966430b53806" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9I-A-{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186325855}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186324248} :answer-field/id #uuid "f00c9e90-925d-5d82-b4f9-f2d77c2b5637" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326651}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0d383f46-698f-5924-8d8d-4466dfa087b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-40168" :question/problem "If $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix},$ then ${A}^{-1}=$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -4-\lambda  & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -3 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((-4-\lambda )(1-\lambda )+3) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+{\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}+{A}^{2}-7A+2I & =O.\end{aligned}

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "29abcc68-95f8-5957-a518-0a35c26f28c7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186486519}} {:db/id 17592186486479 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125140 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "486030d8-debf-5bf3-8646-937755b93331" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2A+{A}^{2}" :db/id 17592186324558} {:answer/id #uuid "7cb39a68-d9fa-5afc-a46e-1646bc050802" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{A}^{2}-A" :db/id 17592186325023} {:answer/id #uuid "8f700b32-f8f5-50c2-8448-a2e3950f6cf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{A}^{2}-I" :db/id 17592186325188} {:answer/id #uuid "d2abfec0-1ad1-5263-bbad-6dc6f697cbf2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2A-I" :db/id 17592186325799} {:answer/id #uuid "ec99ac0a-a7c2-59e7-88f3-37b0874d74a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2A-I" :db/id 17592186326052}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186326052} :answer-field/id #uuid "9ae27e9b-e1c9-591e-ae97-64fbf12bf64f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326497}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "241347e1-d70b-502b-97bb-5ffa2634f0a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-38723" :question/problem "Let $A$ be a $3\times 3$ matrix with the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=-{\lambda }^{3}-2\lambda -1.$ Then, ${A}^{3}=$" :question/worked-solution "Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-4A+I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-4A+I) & =O \\ A-4I+{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =4I-A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=4,$ $q=-1$ and

$$

[{:db/id 17592186079517 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079656 :tutorial/content "When writing out a sum, we often have to write a lot of terms. For example, the following sum has five terms:

$$
S = 2+4+6+8+10
$$

We could just as easily encounter a sum with ten terms, or a hundred terms, or a thousand terms, or even more!

Thankfully, there is a notation called **sigma notation** that allows us to write sums more compactly, without writing every term.

To express the given sum $S$ using sigma notation, we first need to come up with the general term $a_n$ in our sum. Here, the $n$th term of our sum has the form $a_n = 2n,$ where $n$ ranges from ${\color{red}1}$ to ${\color{blue}5}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2(1)=2 \\ {a}_{2} & =2(2)=4 \\ {a}_{3} & =2(3)=6 \\ {a}_{4} & =2(4)=8 \\ {a}_{5} & =2(5)=10\end{aligned}
$$

So, our sum can be written as

$$
S = a_{\color{red}1} + a_2 + a_3 + a_4 + a_{\color{blue}5}.
$$

 

Finally, we use the Greek letter $\displaystyle\sum$ (called "sigma") to denote our summation:

$$
\begin{aligned}S={\sum }_{n\,=\,1}^{5}({a}_{n})={\sum }_{n\,=\,1}^{5}(2n)\end{aligned}
$$

We write the $n$th term $({\color{black}a_n=2n})$ to the right of $\displaystyle\sum,$ we put the first index $({\color{red}1})$ below the sigma as $n={\color{red}1},$ and we put the last index $({\color{blue}5})$ above the sigma.

We can retrieve the expanded sum by substituting all values between $\color{red}1$ and $\color{blue}5$ into the $n$th term, and separating each result with a "$+$" sign, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{5}(2n) & =2(1)+2(2)+2(3)+2(4)+2(5) \\  & =2+4+6+8+10\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** The sum

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{5} 2n = 2+4+6+8+10
$$

is an example of a **series**. A series is what we get when we add the terms of a *sequence* together. In this case, we're summing the terms of the sequence $a_n = 2n.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "27542f45-7f00-500f-8ef4-8f36f6f8b957" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2837 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0d627eef-ef65-5238-9901-90c3400ac3c8" :step/math-academy-id 486637 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079518}} {:db/id 17592186079518 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078569 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078289 :question/id #uuid "be3fc348-da73-5858-bea0-6023bf044e11" :question/math-academy-id "e-4169"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "497072ab-d582-5896-b8a2-12bf1f07c8e9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050652}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186079076} {:db/id 17592186079174} {:db/id 17592186532683} {:db/id 17592186532712}] :knowledge-point/title "Expanding Sums Written in Sigma Notation"} :step/id #uuid "64d8a6fd-3407-5153-8d34-5325bd887b5a" :step/math-academy-id 486638 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079519}} {:db/id 17592186079519 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078570 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078287 :question/id #uuid "50074a6d-1ca5-580b-a716-0a69bcae773d" :question/math-academy-id "e-4166"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dc0a5e10-c402-54cb-80e6-ba4fcc3e9df4" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186079085} {:db/id 17592186079088} {:db/id 17592186532659}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Expressions Written in Sigma Notation"} :step/id #uuid "366dea1e-1586-59cc-a106-0ebd1a1da354" :step/math-academy-id 486641 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079520}} {:db/id 17592186079520 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079610 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to express the following series in sigma notation.

$$
S = \dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2} + \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3} + \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4} + \cdots + \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20} + \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}
$$

To do this, we first examine the numerators and denominators of the corresponding sequence.

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4}, \quad \ldots, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}
$$

Our goal is to find a pattern in the terms. To do this, we note the following:

- The numerators form the following sequence:

$$
{\color{red}1}, \quad {\color{red}2}, \quad {\color{red}3}, \quad \dots, \quad {\color{red}19}, \quad {\color{red}20}
$$

Notice that we have $20$ terms in total. The $n$th term of this sequence is given by

$$
{\color{red}a_n} = {\color{red}n}, \qquad 1\leq n \leq 20.
$$

- The denominators form the following sequence:

$$
{\color{blue}2}, \quad {\color{blue}3}, \quad \dots, \quad {\color{blue}20}, \quad {\color{blue}21}
$$

Since the value in the denominator is always *one more than* the numerator, the $n$th term of this sequence is given by

$$
{\color{blue}b_n} = {\color{blue}n + 1} , \qquad 1\leq n \leq 20.
$$

Therefore, the $n$th term of the sequence

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4}, \quad \ldots, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}
$$

is

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}a_n}{\color{blue}b_n} =\dfrac{\color{red}n}{\color{blue}n+1},
$$

where $n$ ranges from $n=1$ to $n=20.$ 

Therefore, we can express our series using sigma notation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S={\sum }_{n=1}^{20}\frac{n}{n+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check that this answer is correct by writing out the summation in full and checking that we recover the original sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{20}\frac{n}{n+1} & =\frac{1}{1+1}+\frac{2}{2+1}+⋯+\frac{19}{19+1}+\frac{20}{20+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{3}+⋯+\frac{19}{20}+\frac{20}{21}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0c45a9c6-5ee9-5a89-8398-6a3eb37f5f63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13578 :tutorial/title "Expressing Sums in Sigma Notation"} :step/id #uuid "4949bbd4-b355-5948-88e4-04282bd52532" :step/math-academy-id 486644 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079521}} {:db/id 17592186079521 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078571 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078288 :question/id #uuid "b9891d5c-d928-589e-a461-3f0b39fb1b66" :question/math-academy-id "e-4168"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "50fb047f-8c8d-56a6-9093-29a68cd89a90" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078714} {:db/id 17592186078897} {:db/id 17592186079158} {:db/id 17592186244096} {:db/id 17592186532640} {:db/id 17592186532718}] :knowledge-point/title "Writing Sums Using Sigma Notation"} :step/id #uuid "2a86dd84-9a2e-5761-bb0a-6256c5f07a30" :step/math-academy-id 486645}] :activity/title "Sigma Notation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186078688} {:db/id 17592186079517 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079656 :tutorial/content "When writing out a sum, we often have to write a lot of terms. $$
S = \dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2} + \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3} + \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4} + \cdots + \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20} + \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}
$$

To do this, we first examine the numerators and denominators of the corresponding sequence.

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4}, \quad \ldots, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}
$$

Our goal is to find a pattern in the terms. To do this, we note the following:

- The numerators form the following sequence:

$$
{\color{red}1}, \quad {\color{red}2}, \quad {\color{red}3}, \quad \dots, \quad {\color{red}19}, \quad {\color{red}20}
$$

Notice that we have $20$ terms in total. The $n$th term of this sequence is given by

$$
{\color{red}a_n} = {\color{red}n}, \qquad 1\leq n \leq 20.
$$

- The denominators form the following sequence:

$$
{\color{blue}2}, \quad {\color{blue}3}, \quad \dots, \quad {\color{blue}20}, \quad {\color{blue}21}
$$

Since the value in the denominator is always *one more than* the numerator, the $n$th term of this sequence is given by

$$
{\color{blue}b_n} = {\color{blue}n + 1} , \qquad 1\leq n \leq 20.
$$

Therefore, the $n$th term of the sequence

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}1}{\color{blue}2}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}3}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}4}, \quad \ldots, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}19}{\color{blue}20}, \quad \dfrac{\color{red}20}{\color{blue}21}
$$

is

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}a_n}{\color{blue}b_n} =\dfrac{\color{red}n}{\color{blue}n+1},
$$

where $n$ ranges from $n=1$ to $n=20.$ 

Therefore, we can express our series using sigma notation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S={\sum }_{n=1}^{20}\frac{n}{n+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check that this answer is correct by writing out the summation in full and checking that we recover the original sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{20}\frac{n}{n+1} & =\frac{1}{1+1}+\frac{2}{2+1}+⋯+\frac{19}{19+1}+\frac{20}{20+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{3}+⋯+\frac{19}{20}+\frac{20}{21}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0c45a9c6-5ee9-5a89-8398-6a3eb37f5f63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13578 :tutorial/title "Expressing Sums in Sigma Notation"} :step/id #uuid "4949bbd4-b355-5948-88e4-04282bd52532" :step/math-academy-id 486644 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079521}} {:db/id 17592186079610 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to express the following series in sigma notation.
